#2036. Why Newcastle United the football club is an entity which I find increasingly loathsome

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Over nearly forty years of supporting Newcastle United, there are few things more certain than the knowledge that this club will let me down time and again.

In terms of what happens on the field, that is part and parcel of being a football supporter. After all, there are 92 league clubs and it stands to reason that the vast majority of those teams will only watch on, frustrated, while a small minority achieve success.

To that end, on the law of averages we are very fortunate to support a club that has spent its entire existence in the top two tiers of English football, most of my lifetime in the top division and even won a trophy a couple of years back.

So in that context, you can be pragmatic about the failures, enjoy the successes when they come and proudly tell the players in black and white that “we’ll support you ever more”.

Yet it is the club’s activity off the field that really gets my goat. I hate to say it, but while the club has stabilised since the takeover, improved as a commercial entity and enjoyed a bit of silverware for the first time in forever, it has also lost its soul.

“Our fans are the beating heart of Newcastle United,” declared CEO David Hopkinson as he announced the latest season ticket price hike earlier this year.

In 2025, he told the Newcastle United Supporters Trust: “Supporters are at the heart of everything we do.” Meanwhile, chairman Yasir Al-Rumayyan claimed our support “will never be taken for granted” in an open letter to fans back in 2022.

We are absolutely taken for granted. And if we are at the heart of what the club does, it is in the most transactional sense possible – as paying lemmings who are a guaranteed source of income.

Take my experience of trying to get tickets for my sons for the Sunderland game as a prime example.

To be clear, I fully understand that match tickets are at a premium and for this game more than any other, demand would have been huge.

Imagine my surprise, then, when my two sons were seemingly successful in the ballot.

Given the club claim it is a strike rate of one in seven yet this was my eldest son’s first successful ballot in 22 attempts and my youngest son’s first in 15, this was a particularly welcome stroke of luck.

Worse still, because we tried to have him accompany my elder son in the family area, neither were allowed to utilise their ballot success, as my eldest was automatically disqualified when he no longer had a youth to accompany him.

Now I totally understand why these rules exist. Our situation was an unfortunate quirk of when my youngest son’s birthday fell and was an error made in good faith, but it would be very easy for people to exploit this and fill the family section with adults if the club were not vigilant. I get that and I respect that.

That is why I accept when I phoned the Box Office to try to resolve this unforeseen anomaly they were unable to provide us with tickets in that area.

What was less easy to accept was the absolute wall of intransigence and unhelpfulness I was faced with.

Could we get tickets in a different area? “No, you’ve won the ballot in that area so that’s it”.

Why does the website block us from buying the tickets now but did not block us from entering a ballot that it turns out we could never win? “It is your responsibility to enter the ballot in the right area.”

Can we not just have two tickets elsewhere given that the allocation that goes on general sale will be unchanged – we will not be using the two we have won so it will be the same net figure? “No, the policy does not allow that. It would not be fair on other supporters.”

The ballot system is inherently unfair as our strike rate shows – we have had a rare success and now we cannot use it because the system allowed us to enter a ballot we could not win. Is that fair? “I’m not prepared to depart from the policy.”

As anyone who has encountered our Supporter Services will know, escalating the matter to them was about as effective as the experiment of playing Nick Woltemade as a number 8.

Some will say I should not base my view of the club on interactions with a handful of lower paid staff working in the Box Office and Supporter Services. I disagree.

Senior leaders in any organisation set the culture. If David Hopkinson truly believed supporters are the “beating heart” of Newcastle United, he and his executive team would have led the behaviours that set the tone for everyone else.

Interactions with the frontline staff are the very best test for what an organisation really values, and I can tell you now that Newcastle United does not value its supporters beyond the transactional purpose they serve.

Allow me to give another example. Last season, my sister won two tickets in the ballot to take her son to see Newcastle play Bournemouth.

Now my sister is a proper fan. Growing up in Hexham, she spent most of her teen years trying to hang around Causey Hill in Hexham long enough to wave at the passing cars of Mick Quinn, Ray Ranson, Kevin Brock and Mark McGhee, who lived at the top of the road. She even became Roy Aitken’s family babysitter!

She started going to games during the desperate 1988-89 season which ended in relegation and has been a regular at home and away games ever since.

Now living in the south east, getting to home games is an effort and the Bournemouth game last season proved to be a particular trial.

Train delay after train delay resulted in that trip becoming akin to the Griswalds’ trip to Wally World in National Lampoon’s Vacation: rather than it being a day out, it became a mission.

After the first delay they knew it would be tight for kick-off, by the second they knew they would miss some of the first half, by the next they were hoping to get in for the second half, and by the time they eventually arrived it was a case of: “We’ve come this far, we might as well watch the last 10 minutes!”

Off they bombed sprinting up Pink Lane to get to the ground, only to arrive in around the 80th minute and be turned away by the stewards. They presented their tickets, they told them what they had been through, but it was all to no avail. Supporter Services on the day were actually very supportive; those based at the ground said the stewards had made the wrong call and if they called up on Monday they would “see what they could do.”

It turned out, what they could do was never tested: what they would do was absolutely nothing. Supporter Services denied any knowledge of the response they had been given on the Saturday, and virtually accused my sister of making the whole thing up.

“Supporters are at the heart of everything we do”, are they Mr Hopkinson? Well that is not the experience most of us face when interacting with the people you field to manage those relationships.

No, this is a club which has lost its heart.

You need look no further than the utterly dreadful rendition of Blaydon Races which they have forced us to endure on matchdays to understand quite how much the decision-makers at Newcastle United do not understand what our club is. What used to set us apart in home games was the intensity and atmosphere that the crowd brought. Messrs Keegan, Robson and Howe all understood that.

When I was at the depressing Everton game recently, I could not help but think immediately before kick-off ahead of both the first and second halves how the people who make those decisions are strangling the life out of what we are.

If ever there was a way to sap the atmosphere out of the crowd when you need them most it would be by drowning them out with a funeral-march rendition of the Geordie anthem being played at full blast through the stadium speakers. It even killed the Strawberry Corner.

You look at other things – like that dreadful variation on our club badge – and wonder what on earth motivates these people to make the decisions that they do.

The new version looks like some awful re-hash of the original created for a computer game to avoid copyright infringement.

I mean, seriously, was it worth the upset and cost of changing a crest we have known and loved for decades just to introduce that abomination?

I will always love Newcastle United, because it is part of me. That is why, despite Yasir Al-Rummayan’s protestations to the contrary, it is so easy for the powers that be to take us for granted, which they do unreservedly and indiscriminately. We are hooked in by the nostalgia, the memories, the stories, the glorious moments.

Maybe we are motivated by that truly united feeling of togetherness when you are packed into the concourse at any away ground, chanting for 20 minutes non-stop just for each other and the looks on the faces of the bemused home stewards because there’s not a player or opposition supporter in sight.

Perhaps we are driven by the hope, or the sheer unbridled joy of that last-minute winner or a hard-fought victory against one of the league’s elite.

Or for some of us it is just a way of life. Something we did with our mum or dad and now we do with our children, and one day when they are mums and dads they will do with their children too.

In more crass terms, a cynic might say we are victims of Stockholm Syndrome: a condition in which people develop an emotional attachment, affection or loyalty to their captor or abuser.

However much we love Newcastle United, we should never be allow ourselves to forget that it is a love which is utterly unrequited. We are commodities to buy tickets, buy shirts and create an image of fervour that can be sold as a commercial package to the highest bidder.

The members’ general sale tickets for Sunderland sold out within minutes. Yet there is still plenty of room if you are prepared to pay £800 for your ticket, along with  bit of food and the brief musings of one of Keegan’s Entertainers pre and post-match.

While Newcastle United the football team remains something I seem bound to unconditionally love despite all my senses telling me I should not, Newcastle United the football club is an entity which I find increasingly loathsome.

#2035. Writing’s on the wall for West Ham stalwart’s international career

Time catches up with all of us, footballers just the same. Few are given much indication that the writing is on the wall, until suddenly that place which was automatically theirs is going to a younger, fitter, faster team mate – and then, suddenly, without a fanfare, almost always without even a ‘thank you’ –  it is over.

That, sadly, is likely to be the outcome for Czech stalwart and former captain Tomas Soucek who found himself an unused substitute last night after appearing for just five minutes in his countries’ previous game – during which Tornado Tom’s mistake in added time gifted Spain the injury time second goal in their 2 – 0 defeat of the Czechs.

A total of 93 appearances – 42 as captain – and nineteen goals is a pretty stellar international career and for Soucek to have fought his way back from such a bad injury at the World Cup last summer shows his fighting spirit.

You’d think it unlikely that Soucek will make the squad in the March window, after being virtually discarded for the two Nations League games just gone – both of which his Czech Republic side lost.

Hopefully it’ll give the veteran a little more gusto to complete the job and see his West Ham side over the line and promoted back to the Premier League – which would be a fitting swan song for Soucek who’d be 32 next season and probably a bit-part player if the Hammers make it back to the top tier.

At least it’d mean domestically, he could go out at the top. Which he thoroughly deserves after more than 250 West Ham caps.

#2034. ‘We all fell in love with him’ – Hull coach shares what Lewis Koumas was like behind the scenes

A member of the coaching staff at Hull City has spoken very highly of what Lewis Koumas was like behind the scenes during his loan move at the MKM Stadium.

The Liverpool striker spent the second half of last season with the Tigers, playing a part in their promotion to the Premier League with three goals in 18 Championship appearances (including the play-offs).

He’s since become a fixed first-team player at Anfield, being handed five starts among his 14 appearances across all competitions and scoring in the Champions League victory over LASK in October.

Hull assistant coach Dean Holden spoke to The Redmen TV about how Koumas immediately won people over with his humility and hardworking attitude.

The 47-year-old said: “Within a week, everyone fell in love with him, from Stan on the door, the security guy, to the kitchen staff, kit men, the lot. We all fell in love with him.

“You know why? Just because he’s a real humble lad who just wants to be the best he can be and affects people around him in an energetic manner and just loves football.”

Holden went on to share anecdotes of Koumas being out on the training pitch along with Joe Gelhardt ’20 minutes out before everyone else is in the gym’, telling coaches not to ‘sugarcoat’ advice to him, and waiting patiently for his mother to collect him after he scored a late winner for Hull on his debut against Blackburn instead of ‘going out on the town and celebrating’.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

While we’re sure that the Liverpool youngster has been helped by sage advice from his father Jason, who graced the Premier League with West Brom and Wigan, the onus is still on him to put all of that bequeathed wisdom into action, and he’s most certainly doing that.

Andoni Iraola clearly has plenty of faith in the 21-year-old if he’s playing him regularly, even starting him against Manchester City (albeit that Alexander Isak wasn’t fit), and the young striker is repaying that trust with his performances on the pitch.

John Aldridge voiced his belief that the Wales international will ‘play for Liverpool for a long time‘, with Koumas standing out for his indefatigable pressing in the final third, which carries echoes of the beloved Bobby Firmino.

The stories shared by Holden testify to the tremendous attitude of the Reds youngster, who’s remained grounded and earned his place in the first-team squad to the extent that he’s nudged Federico Chiesa further down the pecking order.

We’re sure there’s still so much more to come from the Welshman, provided he can maintain the traits which have taken him this far already and (fingers crossed) avoid any major injury issues.

#2032. Tare discusses new Milan direction, limitations in his role and ‘jealousy’: “Better late than never”

Igli Tare has spoken without holding anything back about his time at AC Milan, explaining his frustration with several things.

When Tare arrived, many Milan fans were happy to see someone with Serie A experience oversee the project and whilst his first season didn’t end how anyone had hoped, he wasn’t seen as a major issue.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

So, when it was announced that he was part of a complete overturning of the management, there was a bit of a surprise, even if it did feel inevitable at one point.

With the overhaul of changes in the summer, one does wonder what Tare would have done differently, especially with suggestions that his hands were tied in the mercato last season. Nevertheless,

Speaking on Sky Sport’s ‘Calcio Unplugged’, Igli Tare revealed all to Gianluca Di Marzio and Stefano Borghi in an in-depth interview about his time with the Diavolo, as Radio Rossonera has relayed.

“Today is the first time I’ve spoken out after all these months. The wound of not having reached the Champions League is still enormous, and since I arrived at Milan – also questioning myself with the type of contract I signed – the objective couldn’t be only the Champions League; otherwise I wouldn’t have understood where I was.”

“It was great because he was the one who convinced me. He had such a huge desire to join Milan. I wanted to video chat before going to see him because I couldn’t believe it. But after five minutes, I knew in my head that he was the player Milan really lacked.

“Not just because of his qualities, but as a man and as a figure that that team didn’t have. He never said no. A photo with a child, an autograph, a meeting, talking to someone… He never said no. These are the things that humility is key to in life.

“I’m proud to have brought a great champion to Milan. In my opinion, if he wants, he can play another two seasons without any problem. He never missed a training session. Sometimes we were the ones to stop him because he was always there, ready. Loving football at that age is truly an honour.”

Is it a characteristic of the champion or is it a generational issue? Today’s champions seem to have a different mentality:

“Today we live in the age of social media. At 16, you’re already a footballer who can earn millions of euros. Living this way, you have the problem of not only managing a player, who is still a child, but you have to manage the business they bring with them: family, agents, girlfriends…

“These are obstacles that didn’t exist back then. We were a generation that played in the streets. Back then, our parents beat us to get us to come home. Today, however, it’s to get them out of the house because they spend all day in front of computers.

“This aspect has been lost a bit, but it’s our fault. Education and discipline are the key to success.”

Fullkrug. He performed poorly in Milan, but in the Bundesliga he’s scoring a lot and is the top scorer. How do you explain that?

“It’s simple. He came to us after a tough time in England, with a lot of scepticism. And then, right away, he broke his toe. No one ever said he’d been having injections on the bone for two months just to train, let alone to play.

“I knew he was a centre forward that the team was missing; given his characteristics and his interpretation of the game, his qualities were unquestionable. Just two years before coming to Milan, he’d played in the Champions League final, playing a key role in a competition with Borussia Dortmund.

“There are situations where, for a player, even a very important one, it matters how you feel. If you feel appreciated, valued, taken into consideration… When you play for a club like Milan, the weight of the shirt is completely different than when you play for other clubs.

“You feel it from the first day you join. I had no doubt that he could be what he’s demonstrating now.”

“We tried to sign him back in June. We made a first attempt. In the final days of the transfer window, another important name we tried to sign was Akanji. The Champions League was crucial for both of them. They turned him down, not because of the club’s importance, but because he wasn’t playing in the Champions League.

“Then the opportunity arose again at the end of August for Rabiot. Defeat against Cremonese? No, we had already decided to bring him. It was just a matter of contract details.”

“It was difficult for us because we decided to change the formation five days before the transfer window closed. Switching from a 4-3-3 to a three-man defense meant we were having a really hard time finding a quality player in the last five days.

“We were a bit unlucky, first with the Akanji story and then with Liverpool’s Joe Gomez… Guehi’s move from Crystal Palace to Liverpool fell through, and at the last minute they—we already had the deal ready, we were just waiting for this to happen—made a step back. And to avoid being left without a central defender at the last minute, we signed Odogu as a promising player.”

On not being able to reach the Champions League and not being able to continue his work at Milan…

“This is the first time today, after all these months, that I’ve spoken about this… The wound of not reaching the Champions League is still enormous. I think that from the first day I arrived at Milan, even in the way I signed—I questioned myself with the type of contract.

“I said, ‘If I have to come only for the Champions League objective, then I don’t understand where I’ve come from.’ Milan has a different story. I had to go through a trial. The disappointment is that those who run the club didn’t understand how much time people needed, which is now being done, rightly so.

“That is to say, it takes several transfer sessions to get a competitive team ready to win. At the beginning, I felt the responsibility to put the pieces together immediately, because after the defeat in the Coppa Italia final the year before, there were some important signs.

“I didn’t know where to start. But I think we did an important job last summer, we sold for a lot and also signed 10 new players. Then you need time to integrate, learn new philosophies and create a cohesive group, hungry to win.

“Until March-April, we were a group with difficulties, but we were at the top of the table. Then in the last 10 matchdays, we had a mental breakdown, also due to other external dynamics, which I don’t want to discuss here, which had a significant impact.

“Internal or external dynamics? External to the team. But we also have some blame: myself first and foremost, along with Max [Allegri].

“We had to be a little more attentive to certain dynamics. We needed to be more present with the team to ultimately lead them to the final result. Isolation is the wrong word; I don’t believe in these things. I believe in teamwork; I believe in cohesion: from the club to the team.

“When this happens, you transmit it to the team. When these situations become possible, you could also see it in the team’s results, because the players are very attentive. Sometimes we think they have other interests, but they pay attention to everything that comes out. They follow everything very carefully and transmit it.

“Instilling serenity… How can you convey serenity? When, in difficult moments, you show that you believe in the project more than before. Sometimes I missed this feeling, a lack of something that could give us the final push.”

But despite this, did you think you could continue? Does this farewell after only a year feel like a stab in the back?

“Look, I would have asked for a round table where we could all sit down together and analyze everything. Then they could have just said ‘no, thanks’… But I respect the decision they made. I accept it with great regret, but I’ve never questioned it because there’s someone above me who has to decide, including for the fate of the club.

“And when they decide to take a different path, you have to accept it. I know things could have gone differently, even much better. I’ll always be a Milan fan, even after an experience like that.”

Was AC Milan a team that needed the constant presence of a manager or coach to avoid letting itself go as it later did?

“The feeling I had at the beginning was that this leadership was a bit lacking. The arrival of Modric—and another of our goals was also Granit Xhaka, Leverkusen’s captain—was precisely to bring real players into the group, with important characteristics and capable of leading others.

“Granit didn’t arrive; Luka arrived, who has a different way of being a leader: he does it in silence and with his attitude on the pitch. I had the opportunity to meet Mike Maignan: an extraordinary guy, a soul who cares deeply about the AC Milan shirt.

“Gabbia is another extraordinary guy; he lives for this club. Rabiot too… His experience spoke for itself. The great disappointment is that I expected something more in terms of responsibility and leadership from Pulisic: he’s a top-class player with unquestionable qualities. But in terms of performance, things happened that I had never experienced in my career…

“Like Gimenez: an extraordinary guy with numbers that spoke for themselves; for a year he failed to score a goal. Then it happened that Pulisic didn’t score for six months. He scored a goal. Then Leao didn’t score for four months.

“Situations that are hard to come by in football have happened… It can happen that you don’t score for a month, two months, but that long a period of time also affected the team’s final performance.

“Losing a match against Cagliari the way we did, 2-1, I think was the worst match of my life. The feeling and the disappointment I felt towards the fans in the stadium that night is something I will never forget for the rest of my life.”

If Cardinale had been the Cardinale he is today, the one who is also physically present, would you still be AC ​​Milan’s DS?

“I can’t answer that question; he has to answer it. I can say that I remember when the Jashari negotiations were going on… I had just landed in Rome and I was very pleased when he called me because he wanted to understand what was happening in that negotiation.

“I explained all the dynamics to him and I really liked that he said, ‘Anything you need, if you have to spend a little more, let me know because I’m here.’ Then during that process I never had the chance to talk to him, even intentionally.

“There were other people above me who I never wanted to bypass. I never had a direct relationship with him, and the possibility of a discussion would have helped everyone. Not me, but everyone. By putting all the problems and dynamics on the table, we could have resolved things much sooner. But I think it’s a new experience for Cardinale.

“He’s had experience in other sports in America. Now he’s done something important, taking responsibility and putting his face on the line. I would have preferred to have had that presence even when I was there because it would have been very useful. But for the Milan, better late than never.

“Now, for better or worse, he will make his own decisions and responsibilities. I think that for him, too, the best interests of Milan come first.”

Was Leao a problem or a resource in your mind?

“I knew him from the outside. When I had the chance to meet him in person, I thought he was an extraordinary guy. I truly loved him as a person, like everyone else. But he was the player from whom we all expected something more. I think football was no longer a priority for him. That’s the key to understanding him.”

“I think a bit about his life outside of football. Music, fashion, things… But I never doubted the sense of belonging he had towards Milan. You could sense that he loved playing for Milan and was suffering from not performing.

“He had many physical problems… First a calf, then a bit of pubalgia… He always played with his hands under control. I always tried to have individual conversations with him more than with any other Milan player.

“Every time I spoke to him, I left with a positive feeling. I sensed that he wanted to. But sometimes wanting isn’t enough.”

Was there a chance that Leao would leave during your summer too?

“A concrete offer never came for him. Regarding the other transfers, it’s not just Tare’s job. When I arrived – even at Lazio – I was a bit alone, but I tried to involve all the members of the club to give him the importance he needed to build a sense of belonging and responsibility. I think I did a very good job, together with Furlani, Ibra, and Moncada.

“We achieved significant sales figures, in a year when we weren’t even in the Champions League. Thanks to the work we did last summer, investments were made this year, with the money we had at the time. I really believe in teamwork.

“I said it even before the Coppa Italia match against Bari; I asked to speak to convey the importance of the work of the people within the club because it was right that way. Then afterwards, it’s human…

“They were coming off a bad year, when two cumbersome figures like Tare and Allegri arrive, and everyone was talking about Tare and Allegri, some disappointment was understandable. I understood the feeling they had, but I could… There was little to do about it.

“For me, it was a new path, a new opportunity. It was essential to work as a team and present ourselves as a real company.”

Aladji Bamba (pictured above with Borussia Dortmund’s Ethan Nwaneri) started in midfield for the France Under 21s at Ashton Gate on Monday night against their English counterparts.

Moore and Mubama put the England Under 21s 2-0 up within half an hour at the home of Bristol City.

Aladji Bamba then one of three French players to be subbed on 64 minutes.

The Newcastle United midfielder watched on from the sidelines as his teammates staged a comeback, scoring in the 80th and 85th minutes.

Elsewhere, a remarkable night in Berlin as Jurgen Klopp saw his Germany side play out their sixth match under his leadership.

His reign had started in dismal fashion with defeat to Greece and a draw with the Netherlands in their opening two Nations League group games.

Jurgen Klopp then made a number of changes which included bringing in Malick Thiaw and in their next three games, Germany picked up seven points from a possible nine and only conceded one goal.

Germany pulling off a stunning 5-0 victory over the Netherlands as they somehow came back from what looked an impossible position to win their Nations League group.

Serbia ended the group without a single point but the other three nations all with 11 points, Jurgen Klopp and his players just edging out the Netherlands and Greece.

#2029. Cody Gakpo sticks up for much-maligned Liverpool teammate with ‘incredible football intelligence’

Cody Gakpo has heaped praise on one of his Liverpool teammates who boasts ‘incredible football intelligence’ and is an ‘extraordinary player’.

The 27-year-old will come up against fellow Reds star Florian Wirtz tonight when Netherlands face Germany in the UEFA Nations League. The Dutchman is also set for a reunion with his former Anfield boss Jurgen Klopp, who takes charge of the home side in Berlin.

LFC’s number 7 has faced some stinging criticism among the British media since his £100m move from Bayer Leverkusen in June 2025, but he went into the international window off the back of scoring one goal and setting up another in the 3-1 win at Crystal Palace eight days ago.

Speaking to the media ahead of tonight’s match, Gakpo was keen to highlight the standout traits of his Liverpool teammate.

The Dutch forward said of Wirtz (via GOAL): “Regarding his situation at the club, I think in his last match he played amazingly. He scored a goal, provided an assist, and was very important for us.

“As a team, we know the quality he possesses; he shows it in every match and training session. He is an extraordinary player.

“Coming to Liverpool with an expensive transfer fee certainly makes the adaptation process in this league not easy for anyone, even for players who have had a 10-year career here.

“However, he has incredible football intelligence. The way he reads and dictates the pace of the game is very important to our style of play. We are very happy to have him.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

With nine goals and 15 assists in 64 games for the Reds so far, it’d be fair to expect a higher return from Wirtz considering his position on the pitch and the transfer fee that the club paid for him.

However, the German is scintillating to watch when he’s at his best, and the win over Palace showed that he’s capable of bending matches to his will when he’s on song.

There have been other standout displays in recent weeks, including the game at Brentford when he created nine chances, and a terrific outing against Villarreal that he marked with a well-taken goal.

There are signs that Wirtz is now properly hitting his stride at Liverpool and primed to consistently turn in impactful performances, something he didn’t do often enough in his first season at Anfield.

Gakpo sees the 23-year-old at close quarters on a daily basis and is perfectly placed to speak about the German’s main qualities. On current form, our number 7 will be pivotal to our chances of success in the 2026/27 campaign.

#2027. Andy Burnham and his comments on the 3pm Saturday blackout got me thinking

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The headline declared that Andy Burnham has urged caution on scrapping the 3pm Saturday TV blackout.

Ahead of this latest international break I was at the Fulham v Newcastle United game, the novelty of it being a rare 3pm kick-off for NUFC.

The BBC article that I was reading, stated: “The blackout originated in the 1960s when Burnley chairman Bob Lord encouraged the EFL to oppose television coverage of 3pm Saturday matches.”

I understand the sentiments expressed by Andy Burnham, as he doesn’t want to be seen as upsetting the lower league clubs who are dependent on match day receipts and the peripheral spending.

However, when you look at the amount of games in the Premier League played outside the Saturday 3pm kick-off, you begin to wonder.

The working man’s game where you could rock up to St James’ Park with a belly full of ale for a 3pm kick-off and pay at the turnstiles are a thing of the past and long gone.

Take a look at the Newcastle United fixtures so far this season and you will see Fulham really was novelty.

In these first five months of the 2026-27 Premier League season only three 3pm Saturday kick-offs for Newcastle United, home to Hull and away to Fulham, plus Ipswich away next month.

All of these Premier League games played outside of the 3pm Saturday slot is a boon for lower league clubs. Due to technology, I can watch Newcastle play at 3pm on a Saturday even when I don’t get a ticket for the match.

But the 3pm Saturday kick-off is such a rarity it has become an irrelevance.

As the Newcastle United games are now shown at an increasingly ridiculous range of times, that frees up Saturday afternoon for me and my mates to go down to Dulwich Hamlet on a Saturday afternoon and have a pint of Peckham pale ale on the terracing while watching live football in the Isthmian Premier League.

So as me and my lad fail to get home tickets for Newcastle United on a regular basis now (no need for tiny violins), we are down the Hamlet on a Saturday afternoon with hundreds of other like minded Premier League team supporting people, who simply want to see live football kicking off at a proper time.

#2026. “Don’t talk about it” – Liverpool star criticised for ‘stupid’ decision on international duty

One Liverpool player has been criticised for making a ‘stupid’ decision while representing his country during the international window.

Andoni Iraola was unsure whether Dominik Szoboszlai would partake in Hungary’s UEFA Nations League fixtures against Georgia and Northern Ireland after the midfielder sprained his knee in the Reds’ 3-1 win at Crystal Palace the weekend before last.

The 26-year-old did end up playing the entirety of his country’s 2-0 victory in Tbilisi on Saturday, although he admitted post-match that he felt a twinge during the warm-up and was close to pulling out before opting to play.

Liverpool-focused journalist David Lynch was critical of the midfielder for playing through the pain barrier to the potential detriment of his club, albeit with an acknowledgement that the Reds’ number 8 would feel duty-bound to represent his nation.

The reporter said on Anfield Index’s Media Matters podcast: “I think there’s no other way to describe this than stupid, really. He could have been a little bit smarter in terms of either not playing the game or, if you’re going to play through the pain in that way, maybe don’t talk about it.

“I don’t think Liverpool supporters are going to like it that you’re prioritising to such a degree. Playing for your country is a massive honour, and particularly when you are the captain, I absolutely understand that. I don’t want to play that down at all.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

This is a classic case of multiple parties having their own vested interests at heart. Hungary were obviously pushing for Szoboszlai to play, and he understandably wanted to come through for his country, whereas anyone of an LFC persuasion would much rather he sat it out.

If the midfielder comes through the match against Northern Ireland tomorrow night and is operating at (or close to) 100% for the Reds’ showdown against Manchester United next Sunday, then he’ll feel vindicated in his stance to continue playing.

However, by admitting that he wasn’t fully fit on Saturday, he’s left himself open to condemnation from Liverpool fans (and reporters, in Lynch’s case) who are justifiably asking why he took the risk of potentially aggravating an existing injury and curtailing his involvement for the club which employs him.

That sense of concern is heightened by Iraola’s team entering a frantic period of 11 matches in 40 days to end this calendar year, plus two more in the first five days of 2027. We can’t afford for Szoboszlai to be out of action amid that thankless fixture schedule.

We get that he didn’t want to let his country down unless he was completely unable to play, but he’s now placed added pressure on himself to be available over the coming weeks for Liverpool, and to deliver the kind of consistently top-class performances that he produced last season.

#2025. “Important to take time” – Gabbia admits January return is possible with right precautions

Matteo Gabbia has admitted that he could return to the field in January for AC Milan, but he doesn’t want to rush back.

It has been a difficult season for Milan, at least where injuries are concerned. In defence, they have had issues reminiscent of the 2023/24 season, where Gabbia had to be brought back from his loan spell at Villarreal.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

This season, though, it seems Gerry Cardinale is going to go down a different route and spend to help Ruben Amorim with his defensive options. Indeed, there have been plenty of rumours about recruitments at the back.

However, Gabbia could again be a key returnee in January, with him hoping to return from injury early in the new year.

Speaking to Sky Sport (via MilanNews) – at an event organised by the Milan Foundation at Milan’s “Arturo Toscanini” secondary school, where they met with several children with disabilities – Gabbia discussed the importance of the event, as well as his recovery.

“It’s wonderful, very enjoyable to spend hours with them. It’s also beautiful to see how they manage to create a group, something that really shows the importance of teamwork, the importance of friendship, even among themselves.

“We’re happy; we thank Fondazione Milan for the project, which is always beautiful and important: we’re happy to be a part of it and we’re enjoying the afternoon.”

Are you able to rejoin the group in January?

“Yes, that could be the time: we’re trying to work hard and do everything as best we can. I obviously have to thank the physiotherapists and the doctor because we’re really doing everything we can every day to try to heal the injury and get back on the pitch feeling good.

“It’s definitely been an unlucky season for me so far: I don’t want it to happen again or for any recurrences, so it’s also important to take the right time, get back in shape, and support the team right now.”

“Although it’s bad for the team that there are so many injured players, we’re together right now, supporting each other and trying to encourage each other through therapy, gym work, and the entire recovery process. Therefore, we’re trying to work as a team this week too, to overcome all the players’ injuries.

“From a personal standpoint, I’m trying to take this time calmly, in the sense that these things are part of sport, part of life, and not all moments are the same.

“This is certainly a difficult time, but it still allows me to stay close to the team, to try to lend my support, even in the good and bad times. That’s what I’m doing, in addition to obviously doing what I can to try to return as soon as possible and make my contribution on the pitch.”

How do you explain the team’s ups and downs?

“I think it’s something we need to get our heads around; we need to understand the importance of every game.

“The other day I heard our coach give an interview in which he said something important: we need to understand that every game, when you don’t win, is taken as a defeat, a heavy defeat. We need to truly understand the importance of every game and approach training to prepare 100%, as best as possible, for every match.

“Therefore, I think this is room for improvement, but I see a group that is really eager to improve, to work, and as a result, I’m sure we’ll be able to fix this flaw as well.

“Although we’ve had a good start to the year in the league and less so in the Europa League, we have plenty of time to improve and have a strong year.”

#2024. Incredible story as Newcastle United teenager creates history with Brazil

Newcastle United teenager Matheos Ferreira has made history in the colours of Brazil.

The exciting 18-year-old winger got his first ever call up for his country this month.

Matheos Ferreira named in the Brazil Under 20s squad for a double header with Peru.

He was an unused sub on Friday when the young Brazil stars won 2-0.

Then on Monday he made history, Matheos Ferreira becoming the first player developed at the Newcastle United Academy to go on to represent Brazil at international level.

The 18-year-old is from Berwick but is eligible to represent the country through his Brazilian father, Thiago.

Not only did Matheos Ferreira make his first ever start for the Brazil Under 20s on Monday, it only took him 14 minutes to score!

The United winger putting Brazil into the lead against Peru Under 20s in Belem.

— Bradley Robson (@bradrobson2605) November 17, 2026

Matheos Ferreira seeing his dream international debut get even better when he also supplied an assist as the Brazil youngsters routed the opposition and won 9-0 against Peru.

The Newcastle United Academy star talked to official NUFC club media from Brazil ahead of his debut: “I had to start training as soon as I got there but I think it’s shown how far I have come as a player because I wasn’t too nervous or anxious… I am doing the thing I love the most, playing football, and it was nice to get on the pitch and train with the squad. It’s been busy! The culture is completely different here but I really like it. We’re having to train in the evening as it is usually over 30 degrees during the day. Since the first training session, I’ve felt very welcome by the lads and the coaches as well.”

Matheos Ferreira also qualifies to play potentially for England and Italy (his mam’s Italian).

The winger joined the Newcastle United Academy in 2020 after playing for Berwick Juniors and Cramlington Juniors and recalled the moment he found out he’d got his first Brazil call up: “My first reaction was just pure joy. I was so happy. My parents wanted to tell me first before I checked my phone but it was still a great moment to share with them, who were both very emotional. I think it’s a reward for how I’ve been playing but also how I’ve managed to conduct myself off the pitch with my recovery, willingness to learn and reflecting on how I can improve on the matches I’ve played in. It’s an amazing achievement but I don’t want this to be the last. I will keep pushing on and try to get that next call-up or progress into the first-team. Once I reach one level, it’s about getting to the next one. It doesn’t stop there. We’ve got the South American (Youth Football) Championship in January and the Under-20 World Cup is next year so I’m pushing really hard to try and get into both squads. I’m doing everything I can to try and make my international debut. It would mean a lot. I haven’t got this big pressure of needing to do well – I just want to get on that pitch, show what I can do and do what I love the most.”

Matheos Ferreira remembering: “My first memory of Brazilian football would be my dad showing videos of Ronaldinho, R9 and Neymar,” he added. “The first game I watched live was at Wembley between England and Brazil and Neymar played. I think it finished goalless though! The interest they showed me and the project they have was a big reason [to accept the call-up]. Brazil is a big country so to be recognised by them is amazing. It’s a big opportunity and an honour to represent them.”

The 18-year-old rising Newcastle United star is buzzing with how the 2026-27 season has kicked off, for club and country: “I’ve really enjoyed the start to this season. The coaches trust me as I’ve been playing in different positions for the Under-21s; wing-back, as a winger or a number ten. I think they know what I can provide for the team. I think its shows the qualities I have. Playing as a right wing-back shows I can defend, put my body on the line and then it’s about showing my strengths going forward. I’ve embraced the challenges of switching positions, thinking about the tactical side of the game.”

A brilliant moment on Monday for Matheos Ferreira and here’s to many more appearances (and goals!) in the colours of Brazil AND Newcastle United.

The Mag Podcast Episode 17: Newcastle United’s 2015-16 relegation with lessons from the past

Published: 16/11/2026 | Duration: 46 mins | Hosts: Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill & David Hutchinson

In Episode 17 of The Mag Pod, we find Jamie, Simon, and Hutch discussing relegation, again! Special focus is on the 2015-16 season when the combined talents of Mike Ashley and Steve McClaren led to the club’s most recent drop to the Championship. So how does the current 2026-27 NUFC situation compare…?

You can play episode 17 on the audio player above or use your favourite podcast platforms including Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, YouTube, and Acast.

Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! Join Jamie, Simon, and Hutch for unfiltered football debate.

Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill and David Hutchinson revisit Newcastle United’s 2015-16 relegation season under the ownership of Mike Ashley, examining the failures under Steve McClaren, the arrival of Rafa Benítez and whether there are lessons to be learned amid the concerns surrounding the current 2026-27 campaign.

The lads also discuss Newcastle United Women’s derby draw with Sunderland and the controversial travel restrictions for the upcoming Tyne-Wear derby.

In the second of three episodes this week, Hutch takes us through another particularly forgettable chapter in Newcastle United’s history. From a disappointing start to the season and a recruitment policy that prioritised potential over experience, to a divided dressing room and a lack of leadership on the pitch, there was no shortage of contributing factors to United’s downfall.

There’s a look back at the performances of Georginio Wijnaldum, Aleksandar Mitrović, Fabricio Coloccini and Moussa Sissoko, as well as some personal memories of the campaign, including a frustrating afternoon at Old Trafford and a particularly miserable pre-Christmas encounter with Aston Villa.

Could an earlier appointment of Rafa Benítez have saved Newcastle from relegation?

The lads discuss the importance of knowing when to make a managerial change, whilst considering the differences between the Newcastle United of a decade ago and the club today.

There’s also an assessment of the increasingly congested Premier League table, the importance of experienced players in a transitional squad and the heroes and villains of the 2015-16 season.

Naturally, a controversial Sergio Agüero goal brings about another argument between Jamie and Simon over the merits of VAR, with all the maturity listeners have come to expect.

Another nostalgic look at a period Newcastle United fans would rather forget, but one which offers plenty of talking points given the challenges facing United today.

#2021. Can Scott Parker Fix What Nuno Couldn’t? West Ham News

Following the international break, Saturday’s clash with Preston North End feels like a pivotal moment in West Ham’s season. The Hammers desperately need to start climbing the table, and while promotion remains within reach, time is quickly becoming a factor.

Promotion from the Championship is not won on reputation alone. West Ham began the season as the bookmakers’ favourites for automatic promotion, but that tag has quietly disappeared.

The dismissal of Nuno and the appointment of Scott Parker signalled a fresh start, although our new manager has had limited time with the squad before the break. What already seems evident, however, is that West Ham’s struggles stem from structural issues rather than shortcomings of individual players.

Kretinsky was not prepared to back Espirito Santo any longer -his tactics and playing style were not working

Parker will be fully aware of the challenges facing his side. The Championship is a division where possession statistics mean very little unless they are backed up by purpose, intensity and results.

Goals have not been the problem. Defensive frailties have been the far greater concern. Playing  Morato at left back never looked convincing, and Saturday’s team selection will be fascinating. With Kilman unavailable due to suspension, Parker must decide whether to pair Mavropanos with Golambekis or Morato.

The absence of a prolific, out-and-out goalscorer has also raised questions. Joel Piroe was recruited to fill that role and, on paper, the logic was sound. He is a proven Championship striker. Four goals and two assists in 14 appearances suggest he is moving in the right direction, but when compared to the division’s leading scorer, Will Lankshear, who has 13 goals, the gap is impossible to ignore.

Ironically, West Ham are the Championship’s leading scorers with 37 goals. Encouragingly, those goals are coming from all areas of the pitch rather than relying on a single player. Yet, there is one player, Jarrod Bowen who has been central to that success, contributing seven goals and leading the league’s assist charts with seven in fifteen matches.

He will go if the club don’t secure promotion, an inevitable outcome should the club not succeed this season.

Perhaps the biggest challenge for West Ham, is psychological.

West Ham arrived in the Championship expecting results to come naturally. As fans we expected an automatic promotion place.

At times this season, West Ham have looked weighed down by expectation. Instead of playing with the confidence of promotion contenders, the team have often appeared nervous and overly cautious, afraid of making costly mistakes.

Scott Parker’s biggest task may not be tactical at all. He must build a mentality centred on resilience and belief rather than entitlement.

If he can transform West Ham into a side that is more aggressive, more robust and better suited to the harsh realities of Championship football, promotion is still very much achievable.

If he cannot, the club’s stay in the second tier could last far longer than anyone at the London Stadium ever imagined. Saturday could be the first real indication of which path they are heading down.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet helped France to victory in the UEFA Nations League on Sunday, but he cut a frustrated figure after their 2-1 win over Turkiye.

The 21-year-old played the full 90 minutes in Bordeaux as Les Bleus finished top of Group A1 to ensure their place in the quarter-finals of the competition, his fourth international appearance after debuting against Belgium in late September.

The youngster has enjoyed an excellent start to his Reds career since moving from Rennes in the summer, but he survived an unenviable moment last night as he carelessly squandered possession in a dangerous area of the pitch before the offside flag came to his rescue.

Speaking after the win for France, Jacquet fronted up to that uncharacteristic error and was grateful that it was ultimately inconsequential for his country.

The Liverpool defender said (via via Made in Foot): “I perhaps preferred my first camp. Tonight, I could have cost the team dearly. Luckily, it was offside! These are little mistakes I need to cut out before I can be satisfied with my performances.”

However, his post-match comments after the win for Les Bleus reflect the standards that he expects of himself, and that ever-demanding attitude will serve him very well as he continues his upward trajectory.

One mistake doesn’t detract from what has been a fantastic year on a personal level for the defender, whose ceiling is incredibly high.

#2019. “Planning approval secured” : Stadium twist could change West Ham’s ownership plans

West Ham United’s window of opportunity to acquire their rented home for next to nothing appears to be fading. With £20 million of losses each year, the ground is a massive white elephant with the main tenant paying next to nothing for it’s bullet proof lease.

Former vice Chair Karren Brady, say what you like about her,  did at least negotiate the deal of the century giving West Ham a rock solid indestructible tenancy for generations to come. As the club were relegated, so the rent diminished leaving the owners to pick up the tab for West Ham’s failure on the pitch: An estimated £2.5 million each year is added to the tax payer burden thanks to the clause existing to reduce costs when West Ham dropped out of the Premier League.

Opportunities existed this summer, so we were told,  for the club to negotiate to buy the stadium, with suggestions that it would take £50 million for the deal to be done.

In the apparent lack of any take up by West Ham’s shareholders, the stadium owners have sought to bump up the former Olympic venue’s value in the meantime, by seeking to increase revenues through obtaining permission from Newham Council for a wider array of entertainment. According to London.stadium.com that effort has paid dividends:

Meaning the revenue which can be generated from the Stadium will be significantly higher, theoretically at least increasing its value and likely heading off West Ham’s options of acquiring it for next to nothing. Possibly.

West Ham’s London Stadium at night: There’ll be more events, louder music and bigger attendances – still won’t make a profit though. Just saying.

However the huge maintenance costs and temporary nature of the upper part of the structure means that even with consent for more events, bigger attendances and louder music, London Stadium is never going to become a lucrative, marketable venue in it’s current configuration.

Someone is going to have to spend hundreds of millions of pounds on fixing it: Like a giant pass-the-parcel game with a huge ticking time bomb of debt at the core of the fancy wrapping, neither West Ham nor the owners want to be left holding the bill when the music stops.

The difference is, the status quo favours the club, not the Greater London Authority who, as it stands, will find it pretty near impossible to turn a profit even with new approvals granted and new events lined up. And as every year passes, the need to spend big, big money on maintenance grows greater. In this instance, West Ham’s board biding their time and kicking it into the long grass for a few years yet is probably the shrewdest course of action. From the football club’s perspective.

#2018. Karren Brady’s New Agency Raises £104m West Ham Question

Former West Ham United vice-chair Karren Brady has launched a new commercial agency alongside fellow former Hammers director Nathan Thompson, specialising in sponsorship, hospitality and commercial strategy. The business, craetively called Brady Thompson, aims to help organisations unlock what its founders describe as hundreds of millions of pounds in untapped commercial value.

According to City AM, the pair have reunited just seven months after departing West Ham, with Brady talking enthusiastically about the enormous commercial opportunities available in sport and entertainment.

I have to say, I find it absolutely incredible that Brady has any sort of influence or clout in a business focusing on sponsorship, hospitality and commercial strategy, considering the Baroness was vice-chair when West Ham recorded losses of £104.2m in their last published accounting period. And that’s before we get onto the rather awkward subject of the London Stadium.

West Ham’s accounts for the financial year ending May 2025 revealed a pre-tax loss of £104.2m, a remarkable turnaround from the previous year’s £57.2m profit.

Now, clearly, not every penny of that loss can be attributed to Karren Brady. Football finances are complicated, and player recruitment, wages, transfer dealings and league performance all have a significant impact.

But she was one of the most senior executives at the football club, and surely the financial performance of the business has to form part of any assessment of her commercial legacy.

Indeed, Claret & Hugh previously reported that Brady had even become directly involved in negotiating transfers during the January 2026 window.

I’ve questioned the timing of her departure before, particularly given the financial difficulties and footballing problems that were developing towards the end of her time at the club.

So forgive me if I’m not immediately convinced by the idea that the same leadership can now teach other organisations how to maximise their commercial potential.

But perhaps the biggest irony of all is the decision to launch an agency specialising in sponsorship when, after ten years at the London Stadium, West Ham and the stadium authorities collectively failed to secure a naming-rights partner for the former Olympic venue.

A Premier League football club, based in London, playing in a stadium with a capacity of more than 60,000, and after a decade nobody managed to get a naming-rights deal over the line.

That wasn’t solely Brady’s responsibility, of course. The London Legacy Development Corporation controlled the stadium’s commercial arrangements, and there were disagreements about the value of any potential deal.

In fact, Brady herself pressed the stadium authorities to pursue naming rights, and the London Assembly has documented correspondence in which she expressed West Ham’s willingness to help secure an agreement.

Nevertheless, the outcome remains the same.

As Claret & Hugh reported last year, the stadium operators were warning that a naming-rights agreement might not materialise until 2028 or beyond.

And in my previous article about the missing £4m sponsorship opportunity, I argued that the failure to secure a partner when the stadium first opened had allowed the London Stadium name to become so established that selling it now would be considerably more difficult.

That is hardly a ringing endorsement of the commercial arrangements surrounding West Ham’s move from Upton Park.

Brady told City AM that unlocking commercial opportunities required imagination, experience, relationships and the willingness to challenge convention.

Nathan Thompson, meanwhile, pointed to his experience negotiating commercial deals from different sides of the boardroom.

I’m sure both have considerable contacts within the business world, and there’s no doubt Brady has spent decades operating at decent levels of football administration.

But contacts and experience are one thing. Results are another.

Perhaps the venture will prove enormously successful. Perhaps they’ll secure the sort of sponsorship agreements that other sporting organisations have struggled to attract.

However, from a West Ham supporter’s perspective, it is difficult to look beyond the £104m loss, the club’s subsequent relegation and the decade-long failure to find a stadium naming-rights sponsor.

When somebody starts offering advice about how to unlock hundreds of millions of pounds in commercial value, I don’t think it’s unreasonable to ask why so much potential remained untapped at the football club they helped run for 16 years.

But hey, if all else fails the new company name of Brady Thompson does sound like excellent branding for a luxury soap should they wish to diversify.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

I remember walking toward stadium a few season when an ad for a skip hire company based in Ilford was displayed on the “largest wraparound screen” in Europe, which itself is still attached to a former Olympic stadium at the time hosting a match involving London-based club. That just about sums Brady up. Lots of talk, but ultimately unable to transform that talk into commercial revenues for the club, in the way that has happened at, say, Spurs. Globally-significant, easily-recognisable brand names were always out of Karren’s reach when she was with us but no doubt she knew where to turn if she ever needed to hire a skip. Hard to magine her new agency being inundated with offers.

I think that’s a tad unfair, haven’t I heard ‘deal of the century’ attributed to her!

Maybe she can approach West Ham to offer us the benefit of her wisdom

Lots of sarcasm intended. But imagine if that were actually to happen!

One has to wonder who will be their favourite client? Mr 40% per chance?

#2016. Jacob Murphy is not our future but he IS the here and now

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

In the grand and often unforgiving theatre of Premier League football, where stars are minted in bursts of brilliance and extinguished by the next transfer window, there are players whose value is measured not solely in highlight reels but in the quiet accumulation of purpose.

Jacob Murphy belongs to that rarer company.

At 31, the Newcastle United winger continues to embody a particular kind of professional resilience—one forged in loans, tempered by reinvention, and now expressed in moments that still make the away end rise as one.

I know, we’ve heard the complaints of many fans and pundits that Jacob Murphy is “not good enough”, that he disappears for long stretches during the match, that we need an upgrade at the position. Maybe. The lad is not perfect or to everyone’s liking but he is my cup of tea. He produces with first-time crosses into the box, always gives 100%, readily gets back on defence, and adds a bit of needed comic relief.

Born in Wembley on 24 February 1995 to parents with roots in NE England, Murphy carried Newcastle in his blood long before he wore the shirt. A boyhood Magpie who grew up visiting family in Gateshead, he and his twin brother Josh cut their teeth at Norwich City’s academy. Together they helped win the FA Youth Cup in 2013. Jacob’s path thereafter was the classic English apprenticeship of the lower leagues: temporary homes at Swindon, Southend, Blackpool, Scunthorpe, Colchester, and, most formatively, a season-long stay at Coventry City in 2015-16 where he scored ten goals and announced himself as a player of genuine threat. Returning to Norwich, he produced a breakthrough campaign of nearly double figures in goals and assists, enough to persuade Rafa Benítez to bring him to St James’ Park in the summer of 2017 for a fee in the region of £12 million.

The early years on Tyneside were not seamless. There were loans—to West Bromwich Albion and Sheffield Wednesday—and the familiar struggle of a young wide player trying to impose himself in a club that was itself searching for direction (certainly, Steve Bruce was not the man to coach him up).

What changed everything was the arrival of Eddie Howe.

Under Howe, Jacob Murphy was transformed from squad option into indispensable operator. He became the energetic wide presence who pressed, crossed, tracked, and, with increasing frequency, delivered. The 2024-25 season marked his high-water mark: eight Premier League goals and a dozen assists, a body of work that placed him among the league’s most productive creators from the flank. He scored in the Carabao Cup semi-final against Arsenal and provided a decisive assist in the final as Newcastle United ended a 70-year wait for a major domestic trophy. For a player once dismissed by some as a useful squad man, it was validation of the highest order.

Murphy’s assets have never been those of the purest technician or the most glamorous dribbler. He is direct. He is tireless. He possesses a left foot capable of bending a ball from distance with sudden, almost unfair venom, and a right foot that can pick out a player in the box. Was Alexander Isak worth the money Liverpool paid without the assists of Murphy? I’d argue that we got top money from the Reds for the rat – and Murphy’s crosses were a major contributor. His willingness to occupy the spaces that make others look better. He crosses with purpose, contributes defensively without complaint, and brings a structural intelligence that managers prize.

In a squad that has undergone significant change—younger faces arriving, senior voices departing—his experience has become a form of quiet leadership. Even after being omitted from the formal player leadership group under new head coach Matthias Jaissle, Murphy has spoken of an unchanged responsibility: to add value, to set standards, to help the younger players understand what the Premier League demands week after week.

This season has been more measured than the explosion of 2024-25. Minutes have been shared; the goal tally has been slower to climb. Yet the importance remains as he’s more dependable than Anthony Elanga and much more experienced that Matias Fernandez-Pardo.

On a November afternoon at Craven Cottage, with Newcastle searching for a response after consecutive defeats, Murphy produced the kind of moment that defines him. Intercepting a loose pass, he drove forward, cut inside, and from fully 25 yards unleashed a curling left-footed strike that left Bernd Leno helpless. The goal was his first of the campaign. It was also a reminder.

Three minutes later Fulham equalised (of course they did) but the point was earned in part because of that individual quality and the industry that preceded it. Days earlier he had provided an assist in a clean-sheet victory at Crystal Palace. The pattern is familiar: when Newcastle need a spark or a measure of control on the flank, Murphy is often the player trusted to provide it.

There is something almost old-fashioned in his story. In an era of astronomical fees and instantaneous celebrity, Murphy has built a career through persistence, adaptation, and an unshowy professionalism. He has scored against Manchester City in his early days, netted a brace against Tottenham (including a scorcher!), contributed to European nights and a first major trophy in generations. He has survived the doubts that accompany any player who does not fit the neatest marketing narrative. Now, with his contract situation under discussion and interest from elsewhere already rejected by the club, he continues to state the obvious with clarity: he knows what he brings.

I am not advocating that Jacob Murphy is our future but he IS the here and now. The best we have at his position and, until we can get in a player with better talent and upside, indispensable for the team this season.

For Newcastle United in this transitional season under Jaissle, that contribution—energy, experience, the capacity for the sudden decisive strike—remains quietly essential. Jacob Murphy does not demand the spotlight. He simply continues to occupy the spaces where the game is still won, one determined run, one precise cross, one unforgettable curler at a time.

In the long narrative of a club that has known both glory and patience, his is a chapter written in steady ink. I think its time to give him some respect. 🎙️ THE MAG PODCAST Ep 15: Fulham frustration, Newcastle United’s season report card and Relegation fears Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! #2015. 9 rule changes to help the referee cut out cheating and make the game fairer

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The referee and his role in what’s wrong with football.

One of the many problems with football in England is the refereeing.

Not necessarily the refs themselves, more the ever-changing guidance and policies they are expected to obey when it comes to their refereeing.

The Premier League is the world’s most popular, watched all around the globe on television in far higher numbers than any other rival.

It is a money-spinning product that cannot afford to lose its pre-eminent position. Those in charge, such as Richard Masters, the Premier League’s chief executive, have millions of reasons to protect the brand.

In his particular case, 2.6 million for the financial year ending on July 31, 2025. That included a £1.1m bonus awarded in part for his help in negotiating record-breaking broadcasting deals with Sky, TNT and Amazon.

That £2.6m remuneration package (as they like to say in the City of London) was £700,000 up on the previous year. Don’t expect any reduction when the 2025-26 figures are lodged at Companies House . . .

The Premier League’s popularity relies on more than having some of the world’s best players. It also depends on the characteristic style of play being distinctly different from La Liga or the Bundesliga or Serie A. Which is where the refereeing comes in.

You might believe a referee’s primary role is to ensure, to the best of his ability, the game is played fairly. You might be right, though I suspect the job of protecting the brand has become the driving force for the man in the middle and his colleagues.

The more free kicks, the less attractive the spectacle. Those in charge of the Premier League cannot afford a stop-start product, because viewer figures are paramount.

Pro Ref knows this, the players know this, the managers know this. That’s why so many fouls go unpunished. Not because the referees should go to Specsavers. They see them and choose to ignore them.

It’s the coward’s way. Or should that be Howard’s Way? Mr Webb, the head of Pro Ref, was pilloried when VAR kept halting the action. He responded by telling the boys and girls at Stockley Park to intervene in only the most extreme cases.

Outcome: a non-decision by the ref is not corrected by the VAR.

The most blatant mistakes are later scrutinised by the Premier League’s key match incidents panel. Its verdicts read like an Orwellian nightmare.

In a typical case, a penalty is not awarded for foul play. The VAR, obeying Howard’s Way, looks and agrees. Days later, the key match incidents panel says: “A penalty was probably the right call but VAR was correct in doing nothing. If the ref had blown for the foul, the VAR would have agreed.”

So there you have it. Whichever call the referee makes is correct. It must be, because the VAR backed him up. Reminds me of the olden days when the referee’s decision was final.

Before each season starts, changes are announced to the way the laws of the game will be enforced. Among recent initiatives was the five-second countdown on throws and goal kicks if the referee detected time wasting. They are rarely enforced because the threat of being penalised has encouraged quicker play, as intended. There’s also a 10-second limit for a substituted player to leave the field.

Nobody would argue against those changes, though they smack of window dressing when much more important problems are being ignored. Here are just a few suggestions to make the game fairer.

1. Warn any player who refuses to retreat 10 yards promptly from an opponent’s free kick. The second time he or a teammate does it, book the offender. Third time, red card.

2. Issue a yellow card for pushing whenever no attempt is made to play the ball.

3. Award a throw-in to the other team if the ball is not released from behind the head. Or if both feet are not grounded behind the touchline. Or if the throw is taken more than two yards forward of the right point. Players know.

4) Book any player who pulls an opponent’s shirt, shorts or socks.

5) Stop players taking free kicks from the wrong spot. If they do it again, book them. Keepers in particular move the ball up the field or towards their goal with impunity, knowing the referee will do nothing.

6) A yellow card for all offences of dissent, either physical or verbal, directed at the referee or his assistants. Including the captain.

7) An automatic card to any player who dives. In the opponents’ penalty area, make it a red.

8) Add on at least one minute for every goal celebration.

9) Play an advantage if there is the chance of one but go back and book any player who has fouled off the ball.

You might think there would be a blizzard of yellow and red cards. I believe the far more likely consequence would be a massive reduction in gamesmanship, cheating, time wasting and other examples of the dark arts that are blighting the beautiful game.

Once players realised they couldn’t foul with impunity, they would quickly learn to play the game as a sport, rather than as a cynical win-at-all-costs exercise.

#2014. Jurgen Klopp ‘shocked’ by Florian Wirtz as Liverpool star excels in Germany romp

Jurgen Klopp has proclaimed Florian Wirtz as an ‘extraordinary footballer’ after the Liverpool playmaker’s starring performance for Germany on Monday night.

The 23-year-old scored twice in his country’s 5-0 drubbing of Netherlands in the UEFA Nations League, with his first goal seeing him provide a stunning curled finish from outside the penalty area.

The Reds’ number 7 now has four goals and an assist from his last four international caps, whilst also scoring and assisting in his most recent appearance for his club when they beat Crystal Palace the weekend before last.

Speaking to the media after the match in Berlin, Klopp admitted that Wirtz took him by surprise when he began working with the Liverpool star, whose qualities out of possession were lauded by the former Anfield boss.

In quotes relayed by Sky Germany reporter Patrick Berger on X, the 59-year-old said: “I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer.”

“We’ve also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he’s so vocal. He’s the first pressing player, can press two players without getting tired.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Klopp’s lofty praise of Wirtz comes just after the 23-year-old’s Liverpool teammate Cody Gakpo hailed his ‘incredible football intelligence‘, and the Reds’ number 7 has been busy confounding his doubters in recent weeks.

He’s been subjected to some heavy criticism since his £100m move from Bayer Leverkusen in June 2025, with Jamie Carragher even calling for him to be dropped from the starting XI, but right now he’s one of the first names on the team sheet for club and country.

In addition to his two goals against Netherlands on Monday, he won three duels, completed 88% of his passes and recorded a 100% dribble success rate (Sofascore), delivering a fine performance throughout the night.

Klopp has worked with several world-class players throughout his managerial career, so for Wirtz to leave him ‘shocked’ with his quality just shows how much talent the Liverpool playmaker possesses.

The coach’s comment about the 23-year-old being vocal are also noteworthy – could he develop into a potential future captain for the Reds, provided he stays at Anfield for the long-term?

Our number 7 has copped his share of flak since coming to England, but right now he’s undoubtedly a crucial figure for club and country.

#2013. Why journalists’s claim of imminent departure will go down just fine with fans | West Ham News

When relegation reality kicked in and the dust settled, fans waited for players to confirm their intentions as far as playing in the second tier were concerned. The first two to break cover were inevitably Jarrod Bowen and Tomas Soucek who made their loyalties pretty clear.

Others followed including Mavropanos and Castellanos – and fans thought there was the spine of a team that would flourish in the Championship. Supporters renewed their season tickets in their tens of thousands, hoping that West Ham would dominate the division after two terrible years of being rooted at the foot of the Premier League.

West Ham sit in ninth having fired Nuno, (the Championship Manager of The Month for September, remember) and the ‘match winner’ we all expected Taty Castellanos to become has simply not materialised.

Castellanos: All ‘attitude’ and no ‘action’.

So much so that now there’s a realisation from Scott Parker that West Ham need a new striker and news just today from Taty’s homeland suggests he’s made his own mind up that it is time to walk away: Argentine journalist Renzo Pantich (with some 250k followers) confirms it:

“Referring to a possible departure from West Ham, Pantich had said: “He wants to leave West Ham, many have already begun to give it as a possibility or as if River laid his eyes.”

Pantich separated the possibility that Castellanos wanted to leave the English club from his intention to return to South America. About his future, he said: “Well, the footballer would not plan to return to South America, in fact he rejected an offer to Flamengo and also plans to stay a little longer in Europe.” (Elintransigente.com)

Which certainly suits the club and its own fans: Europe, specifically the Premier League, is where the money is that would allow West Ham to recoup most if not all of their outlay.

Unlikely, you’d think, that Taty would find a Premier League side willing to take him after failing so spectacularly in the Championship?

Knowing the craziness of football, it is probable there’s already a manager out there who thinks they can unlock his talent and his goals. They might need to work on his attitude too.

Castellanos has been one massive disappointment for supporters this season, with his goals, assists and build-up play having deserted him, the only thing remaining is the scowl and the attitude.
