#1962. Andy Robertson has ‘no time’ warning for Pocognoli’s Scotland as record-breaking night turns sour

Andy Robertson issued a warning that Scotland do not have time to get things right under Sebastien Pocognoli after his record-breaking night was spoiled by a 4-0 defeat in Switzerland.

The Tottenham left-back became Scotland’s most-capped player by making his 103rd appearance in St Gallen to eclipse the previous milestone of 102 caps set by Kenny Dalglish 40 years ago.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

However, the captain’s personal achievement was overshadowed by a dismal performance and result that left Scotland with a record of seven points from a possible 18 and a third place finish in Nations League Group B1.

Switzerland were gifted a first-half opener when Lewis Ferguson turned a harmless cross into his own net before Scotland allowed the roof to cave in by conceding twice in the opening six minutes of the second half.

Strikes from Winsley Boteli and Alvyn Sanches put the hosts 3-0 up before Zeki Amdouni added a fourth in the final minute to increase scrutiny on Pocognoli after a less than impressive start to his tenure.

"I thought first half we were in the game," Robertson said. "We lost a stupid goal but I thought we had chances and could easily have been one-each at half-time.

"We talk about it at half-time to say keep going and by 50 minutes we're 3-0 down. That cannot happen in international football.

"We were playing against a good team but we were in the game in the first half. We have to do it for 90 minutes. Then you're 3-0 down at a tough place. A really tough night for us."

Pocognoli has yet to convince the Tartan Army that he is the right appointment after succeeding Steve Clarke, who resigned after seven years in charge following Scotland's World Cup exit.

Asked if it will take time for the 39-year-old Belgian's methods to bear fruit, Robertson warned: "I don't think you've got time in international football. You have to do it.

"Are those supporters who have travelled everywhere going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden that are going to be critical, and rightly so, going to give us time? No. We've not got time. The players don't have time. We have to step up.

"We now have a long break until March which is not a good thing. It's going to be a tough one to swallow."

#1961. CorSport: Fontanella-Khan up and running within Milan’s management – his background and role

James Fontanella-Khan is up and running with his new position at AC Milan, following an interesting background which includes the former Rossoneri man Alberto Gilardino.

It was in the middle of September that various outlets reported that Fontanella-Khan was joining Milan’s management as the new Chief Corporate Affairs Officer. Two months have passed since and the 43-year-old is now up and running with his new gig.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

He has been spotted among the top brass in the stands of San Siro during the most recent games and he was also present at the dinner Gerry Cardinale hosted before the derby. In other words, he’s not exactly working remotely, instead expected to spend most of his time in Milan.

Today’s edition of Corriere dello Sport (via MilanNews) has taken a closer look at Fontanella-Khan, who has various valuable experiences to rely on in his new gig. Most recently, he was the US Financial Editor for the Financial Times, even moderating some conferences that Cardinale spoke at.

Before making waves in the US, however, he actually grew up in Italy and even played football himself. He was a goalkeeper in Piacenza’s youth team, reaching the Primavera of the club, and he was even a teammate of Alberto Gilardino (the former Milan striker) at one point.

After deciding that football wasn’t his path in life, he left Italy to start an internship for the Financial Times in London. He worked his way up and remained at the newspaper for over 20 years before accepting the Milan gig.

As for his role with Milan, according to Corriere dello Sport, he could be described as a General Manager. He handles communications, politics (he will be present at the League assemblies), and represents the club at various events.

Part of his goal is to connect the US mentality of the Rossoneri ownership with the Italian identity of the club, partly relying on his background as a footballer and Milan fan.

#1960. Scotland talisman sets out March plan of attack, defends Pocognoli and names what team must improve

Scotland midfielder John McGinn has warned his international teammates not to hide behind fans’ formation frustrations after pressure mounted on head coach Sebastian Pocognoli following a 4-0 defeat to Switzerland.

McGinn, 31, was powerless to resist as Scotland’s poor Nations League campaign ended in a dismal defeat against a heavily rotated Switzerland side. A Lewis Ferguson own goal opened the scoring early on, before second half strikes from Winsley Boteli, Alvyn Sanchez and Zeki Amdouni saw the hosts coast to victory in St Gallen.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

A third defeat in Pocognoli’s first six games, the result meant Scotland ended their Group B1 campaign in an underwhelming third place, leaving many supporters frustrated by Pocognoli’s refusal to turn away from a rigid 3-4-2-1 formation, with some believing that he is struggling to adapt his tactics to fit the strengths of the squad.

However, Aston Villa captain McGinn has refused to blame Pocognoli, insisting that formations and the new manager’s methods become irrelevant if the players aren’t displaying their qualities on the pitch.

“Obviously the trajectory of results means it’s impossible for me to say yes,” said McGinn when asked if Scotland are on the right path. “But we have been here before, and unfortunately we’ve been in moments where you need to stick together, show your qualities. Players need to come into the group and add more. And you need to turn results around, which we have shown before.

“The manager can’t kick the ball for us. It’s up to us to make the right decisions in those moments, execute it, show a bit of quality, and be a lot better on the ball and off the ball. And that doesn’t matter what tactics you have or formation you play, you need to be a lot better in yourself and not a lot of us can say that tonight.”

The 4-0 hammering was Scotland’s final game of the calendar year, with the team not due to play again until their European Championship 2028 qualifying campaign begins in March. Desperate to qualify for their third successive Euros, McGinn set out a plan of attack for the new year and insists the best way for the squad to support Pocognoli is by improving their performances on the pitch.

“We’ve qualified for three out of four major tournaments,” said McGinn. “If we’re going to qualify for a fourth, we need to be much better, We know that. We know what it takes, but you don’t have time in football as a bunch of players to do that. So, come March, we need to be a lot better and improve.”

Meanwhile, Pocognoli defended the performance against the Swiss, and insisted the scoreline did not reflect the action on the pitch, saying: “The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don’t think it’s a reflection of the game, if I’m really honest and objective. I think we had some very good moments in the game, we started the game like we wanted, aggressive away from home. We played a good first half, we created chances, we were dominant in some moments in the game.”

#1959. Chelsea rejected by Real Betis star with £25m release clause

Chelsea failed with an approach to sign Real Betis winger Jose Antonio Morante, according to reports in Spain.

The 19-year-old made his first-team breakthrough with Real Betis earlier this year and has made three appearances for the Spanish club this season.

In the summer, Morante was a key part of the Spain squad which won the UEFA European Under-19 Championship. He finished in the Team of the Tournament with five of his Spain teammates and ended the tournament as the joint-top scorer with four goals.

According to ABC Sevilla, Chelsea monitored Morante during the European Under-19 Championship and made an approach to the winger’s representatives in the summer transfer window.

However, Morante is understood to have personally turned down a move to Chelsea as he wants to become a first-team regular with his boyhood club Real Betis.

#1958. ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

“We did the first one quite well in a lot of moments but the compete part – especially in and around our box – was not to the standards to win a football match against a good side. It’s better to give them [the goals away] in a friendly match than an official match. It’s always good when you lose a match in pre-season because it creates a bit more fire in the belly.”

Kepa Arrizabalaga will not want to watch Betis’s first goal back in a hurry. The Arsenal goalkeeper may have got a slight nudge as he came for the ball at a corner but he was all over the place and never looked even in the vaguest control of the situation. Rodrigo Riquelme scored at the far post after the ball sailed over the keeper. Arteta called it a “really sloppy goal”. With former Leeds goalkeeper Illan Meslier having arrived on a free transfer as back-up to Raya, Kepa faces an uncertain future at Arsenal. Moments like this will not help his cause.

He did not feature much last season but is probably best remembered for his torrid showing in the Carabao Cup final defeat by Manchester City in March. He looked as unconvincing here as he did then, as the former Chelsea goalkeeper also sliced a clearance in the build up to Betis’s third goal. Before then, Kai Havertz had turned over possession cheaply from which Nelson Deossa set up former West Ham midfielder Pablo Fornals to score.

Arsenal need more creativity and firepower in attack, hence the interest in Vinícius and Atlético Madrid’s Julián Alvarez. Viktor Gyokeres again looked rather limited here and the likes of Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze are also still to report back. Yet one of the few, brighter aspects of Arsenal’s performances was the sight of the regal looking Riccardo Calafiori marauding forward from a very nominal left-back role.

If Arsenal are going to play more adventurously this season and try to ratchet up things in the entertainment stakes then Calafiori could have a big role to play, as long as Arteta can keep him fit. He can be a potent weapon galloping forward and there were clear glimpses of that here. Harnessing that talent while not compromising too much defensive security may be one of the manager’s challenges.

Louie Copley had only been on the pitch for nine minutes – a half-time substitute for Ben White – when the 19-year-old midfielder went down largely unchallenged with what looked like a troubling knee injury. Arteta admitted afterwards that the way the teenager fell to the ground was a concern and he looked in visible pain and distress as he was treated by the medical staff before being helped off the pitch.

The fear will be of some kind of ligament damage and Arteta confirmed Copley would be scanned on Thursday. “Quite worried to be fair for the kid because the mechanism doesn’t look very positive and the symptoms that he already has,” the manager said. “So we are going to have to wait and see for tomorrow’s scan. Touch wood that is not a bad one.”

🌴 @RealBetis_en's Hector Bellerin reacts to a 3-1 preseason win over his former club Arsenal"I spent 10 years over there always trying to help and see Arsenal where it belongs, and it's nice to finally face them with them being in that position" 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/er3YtAysQb

“It is another opportunity for fitness. Coming into games against teams of good quality, it is important we get good fitness. It is a chance to build momentum for the season ahead. Play is halted as Copley has been down for a little while clutching at his left knee. He got his studs stuck in the ground and went down in some pain. The medics come on to check that left knee. He only came on at half-time but his night is over not even 10 minutes into the second half.

Nwaneri catches Bernal and if this was a competitive fixture than I think Nwaneri would perhaps have been booked for that challenge.

Those raft of changes from Mikel Arteta at half-time have seen just four of their starting XI remain on the pitch; Kepa, Calafiori, Lewis-Skelly and Nwaneri.

Arsenal have a corner early on in this second half as Vieira’s shot from distance deflects behind. The delivery from the left has too much on it, going over the heads of all the Arsenal players in the box, and Betis are able to clear.

Mikel Arteta has made a whole host of changes, which includes the likes of Jesus, Martinelli, Gabriel and Vieira coming on. Betis have brought the former Real Madrid man Isco on at the break.

Arsenal are closing in on the signing of Newcastle and Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimaraes in a deal worth £75m. One midfielder coming into Arsenal is set to see another depart as Dane Christian Norgaard closes in on a move to Everton after just one season at Arsenal.

Premier League champions Arsenal continue their preparations for the new season as they take on Spanish side Real Betis at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin, with this being the first-ever meeting between the two sides. This is the first time Arsenal have played a pre-season game in Dublin since August 2018, when they drew 1-1 with London rivals Chelsea, with Arsenal winning on penalties.

Arsenal beat Girona 4-1 in their opening game of pre-season, with new signing Christos Tzolis on the scoresheet in his first appearance for the club. After today, Arsenal have three more games, including the Community Shield, before they kick off the defence of their Premier League crown at home against newly-promoted Coventry on opening night of the new season. They are closing in on a deal for Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes, who is set to become one of Arsenal’s most expensive signings. Mikel Arteta’s side have been dealt a blow ahead of the season with the news that France centre-back William Saliba will miss an extended period due to a back injury. The likes of Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Noni Madueke are still yet to return after their World Cup exploits.

Real Betis, under the management of former Manchester City boss Manuel Pellegrini, finished fifth in La Liga last season and have therefore qualified for this coming season’s Champions League after a 20-year absence from the competition. Pellegrini has led Betis into European competitions for five consecutive seasons, which includes losing the 2025 Europa Conference League final to Chelsea. They have been busy in pre-season action already having played five games up to this point. They have won four of the five, including a 4-0 victory over Lyon, with just one defeat coming against Granada.

They have a number of former Premier League players in their ranks, including Antony, Giovani Lo Celso, Pablo Fornals and former Arsenal man Hector Bellerin. Real Betis have already played a number of friendlies as they build up to the start of their season, which begins on August 21 when they take on Real Sociedad.

#1957. Celtic ‘platform’ can revitalise forgotten star as Man Utd move labelled a mistake amid Bellingham comparison

Celtic have been hailed as the perfect destination for England international Jadon Sancho to reignite his career and shine again as he continues the search for his next club.

Sancho, 26, is currently a free agent after his contract at Manchester United expired in the summer, but was part of the Aston Villa squad that won the Europa League with a 3-0 win over Freiburg after spending last season on-loan in the Midlands. He also won the Conference League with Chelsea in the previous campaign.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

A £73million signing for Manchester United in the summer of 2021, Sancho was viewed as one of Europe’s most promising talents during his time at Borussia Dortmund, scoring 50 goals in 137 appearances and forming a lethal partnership with former Signal Iduna favourites Marco Reus, Erling Haaland, and Jude Bellingham.

However, the pacey winger was never able to replicate his Dortmund form at Old Trafford, culminating in a high-profile public fallout with former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag over training performances in September 2023. Sancho spent the following three seasons away on loan from the club before being released, but he’s now been urged to consider Celtic as his next destination by former Parkhead icon Paul Lambert.

“Jadon Sancho to Celtic? You could see something like that working,” Lambert told BetVictor. “I don't think he should have left Dortmund for Man United. I thought he should have stayed, like Jude did. Like I said, I don't think Jude Bellingham would be the player he is if he'd stayed in Britain. He made that move to Borussia Dortmund and propelled himself. I think his brother Jobe is the same, a terrific young player.

“Leaving Britain to play in Germany at Borussia Dortmund was the right decision. Would Harry Kane have won the Ballon d'Or if he was still at Tottenham? Absolutely no chance. He went to a club with incredible standards and a great league, and it propelled him. I'd argue with anyone until I'm blue in the face, would Jude Bellingham be the player he is if he went straight from Birmingham to Real Madrid?

“Absolutely no chance. Borussia Dortmund gave him the platform, and Jobe is the same. I saw him play against Bayern Munich at the weekend and he was excellent. Moving abroad makes you grow up, and if you pick the right club, your game improves tenfold. Looking back at Jadon going to Man United at that point, I would have stayed in Dortmund.

“As long as Jadon gets his creative head back on, because he's definitely a threat when he has the ball. He's got to get that back. You could see it happening, and he wouldn't be adverse to it as long as he has the fire and hunger, because he has the ability. He just has to pick the right club to give him that platform to express himself again, that could be Celtic.”

#1956. Man Utd accelerate plans to sign £67m star as Mauricio Pochettino’s first January transfer

Manchester United plan to make a move for Como star Nico Paz as early as the January transfer window and make him one of Mauricio Pochettino’s first signings at Old Trafford.

Pochettino has signed a two-and-a-half year deal in Manchester with hope he can lift the club after their worst start to a season in 40 years.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss will be backed in the January window with up front and left-back believed to be two areas that could be strengthened.

With Bruno Fernandes’ long-term future in doubt, United are also monitoring Argentina international Paz.

The 22-year-old tormented Michael Carrick’s side in the Champions League last month, scoring twice and providing an assist in a 4-1 victory having grown into one of Serie A’s brightest talents under Cesc Fabregas.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

Paz joined Como in 2024 from Real Madrid with Los Blancos retaining a £67million buy-back clause which can be activated next summer.

While recent reports have suggested United’s interest in Paz is with a summer move in mind, Argentine newspaper Clarin now claims they could bring plans forward, with the attacking midfielder now on their shortlist of January targets.

Aware of Real’s summer buy-back clause, the report states United could accelerate negotiations and use Pochettino’s arrival to convince him to make the move to Manchester in early 2027, beating Real to the punch.

Real explored the possibility of re-signing Paz last summer with the player telling Jose Mourinho he wished to stay in Italy to continue his development.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

Marca meanwhile add the possibility of a move to the Premier League appeals to Paz’s representatives although Como’s transfer position and Real’s intentions will be a deciding factor.

The Argentine youngster has scored six goals and provided eight assists in 14 appearances for Como this season.

United’s interest in his services comes as their captain Fernandes considers his future in Manchester having rejected two offers of a new contract.

His current deal expires at the end of the season although United do have the option to extend that by a further 12 months.

#1955. Ex-Celtic and Hibs boss forced to quit managerial role for a second time due to ‘health issues’

Former Celtic and Hibs head coach Tony Mowbray has been forced to step down from his role at EFL Championship outfit Blackburn Rovers due to health issues.

Mowbray, 62, returned to the dugout at Ewood Park for a second time in the summer, having previously managed the club between 2017 and 2022, where he led Blackburn to 13th in the table after winning six of his first 15 games in charge of the club.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

However, in an emotional statement on the club’s official website, Mowbray has now confirmed he has departed his role as manager, with assistant Mike Dodds placed in temporary charge.

Previously head coach at Birmingham City, he stepped away from his role at St Andrew’s in early 2024 due to health reasons, later revealing he had been undergoing treatment for bowel cancer, though he was eventually given the all-clear following treatment.

A statement on Blackburn’s website read: “Unfortunately, due to health issues, I have to step back from my role as head coach of Blackburn Rovers. I'm immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I've loved working with them.

“Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you've given me. It's been a pleasure working alongside you. To the fans, thank you for the way you've supported me and the team this season. I've always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me."

In response, Blackburn chief executive officer Steve Curwood said: “Tony's passion for the club and his professionalism are clear to see, but it is his kindness and the care he shows for players, staff and those around him that mean so much. Our priority now is to make sure he feels that same care and support from all of us. We will support him and his family in every way we can.”

During his successful management career, Mowbray led West Bromwich Albion and Blackburn to promotion and, more recently, took Sunderland to the EFL Championship playoffs in 2023. At Hibs, he won the Scottish Football Writers' Association manager of the year award, spending two years at Easter Road between 2004 and 2006.

He returned to the Scottish Premiership with Celtic, whom he represented over 75 times during his playing career in the summer of 2009. However, a lack of domestic success saw him relieved of his duties the following March.

#1954. Tottenham urged to consider shock transfer move for £64m Arsenal star

Tottenham should consider a shock transfer move for out-of-favour Arsenal striker Viktor Gyokeres, according to former manager David Pleat.

Roberto De Zerbi’s side won three of their four matches prior to the international break to move up to 11th in the Premier League table.

Despite their lavish summer spending, Spurs still lack a reliable goalscorer, with centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke the only player to have scored more than one league goal so far this season.

And while he is not blown away by the options on the market, Pleat suggested that Spurs look to their arch-rivals for a solution to their lack of goal-scoring threat.

‘There aren’t many out there, there’s a very small amount of strikers,’ he told The Last Word On Spurs.

‘Are you going to buy Lankshear back now for £50 million? He’s the top scorer in the Championship, our boy.

‘So where are you going to get? Are Arsenal going to give us someone like Jesus, or someone they don’t want? He’s gone already, but, Gyokeres, perhaps. Who else is there?’

‘[Brian] Brobbey gave us trouble… [Dominic] Calvert-Lewin is very good in the air but had injury problems.

‘When you are signing a striker, it’s about what type of striker. Is he exceptionally good in the air, is he a bully-type striker like Delap or is a clever front player, more like Havertz.’

Gyokeres arrived for big money from Sporting CP last season, but has started just one league match this campaign after falling beneath Kai Havertz in the pecking order.

‘I want to [stay],’ he told reporters while away on international duty with Sweden. ‘It feels good when I’ve played. We’ve won most of the games. It was a tough loss in the cup [Fleetwood].

‘Otherwise it’s felt good for myself and the team. I’ve been doing well lately when I’ve been playing. Right now it feels good.

‘The communication with Arteta is good. We talk about football and how we should play. Before a match, if I’m going to start, we talk about the opponents and what I should think about.’

#1953. Gila discusses his mental health journey, perfectionism and current state: “Changed my perspective”

In the latest episode of AC Milan’s The Chamber series, Mario Gila was the guest and spoke about the positive mental health journey that he’s currently on.

It was last month that Milan unveiled their new series, called The Chamber, which focuses on the mental health of the players at the club. Luka Modric was the first guest, a perfect start in many ways, and the second episode has now been published with Mario Gila as the guest.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The concept, in case you’re not familiar, is that the players are placed in a ‘Chamber’ with no outside noise for a few minutes. Then, they are interviewed by the host Luca Casadei, who focuses on the mental state of the players.

As said, Gila was the guest in the most recent edition and he has a lot to say, having been on a mental health journey in the last few years. Indeed, after hitting ‘rock-bottom’ at Lazio, he found a way through and is now very happy.

How are you feeling right now? [after being in the chamber, editor’s note]

I feel very peaceful, I feel really good here. I think experiences like this are also closely linked to how a person feels and where they are emotionally at that moment. And I think it amplifies everything… a little. I wanted to experience it to the fullest when they told me about it.

I think when there are no outside influences clouding your mind that’s when you connect most with yourself. That’s why I closed my eyes. I wanted to feel as deeply as possible what was inside me and how my mind works in moments like this.”

What did you feel during this experience?

Well, I really enjoyed it because I felt so peaceful. I felt completely at ease, and it was an experience I’ve rarely had before. I’m someone who likes to meditate, to reconnect with myself, and I’m interested in spirituality, it’s something I genuinely enjoy.

“And I felt so much peace, so much peace because with everything so quiet, such complete silence and being in touch with myself, it really is an experience I’m not sure I’ll ever forget. I really liked it.”

Speaking about yourself, are there moments when you’re alone, away from the public eye, away from everyone expecting something of you, when you take some time just for yourself? I’d like to know what you feel, who you are emotionally in those moments.

It doesn’t happen to me often because, whether you like it or not, footballers tend to have very active minds. It’s a profession that takes a huge mental toll.

“But I try, for example, during holidays or whenever we get some time off, to find situations where I feel, well, maybe not exactly like in that chamber, but where I can connect with myself, where I can rediscover that Mario who sometimes gets a little lost because of the job he does.

“And in those moments, well, I feel at peace, I feel that connection with myself, I feel like a person. Because in our profession, whether we like it or not, we lose touch with ourselves a little. And that’s what I’m trying to achieve when I’m alone with myself.”

You told me that because of the job you do, you’re always very focused. I wanted to talk about control because I’ve heard you say you need to have everything under control.

Yes, I think that, given the way I see the profession and the position we footballers are in, I think it may not seem like it, but you have a lot of things to manage. How you behave off the pitch, you’re a footballer 24 hours a day, your diet, physical preparation, training sessions, the physio.

And it’s like… I have to keep everything perfectly under control so that at the weekend or in a midweek match I’m at my best.  So the profession itself pushes you to keep everything under control and if you’re also someone who likes that and believes things should be that way, you take it even further.

“And in those situations, I feel comfortable when everything’s under control.”

Is that just at work, or does it apply everywhere, with your family, your friends, always needing to have everything under control?

I’ve been like that with my family too, with my teammates, with my friends, but I see my personal life differently now. I didn’t before. Because perfection is exhausting.  In the end, so many expectations… Striving for perfection wears you out.

“I think that, to a certain extent, it’s boring. You don’t get to see the real person, their authentic self. So that’s how I’ve been for much of my life. I’m young, but I’ve been like that. Now I’m beginning to understand better that everyone is different, that every moment is different, and to appreciate that more, that authenticity.

Did you used to feel weak when you weren’t in control? Vulnerable?

Now, though, you’ve realised it’s a strength?

“Yes, yes, yes. I understand that people and situations aren’t always as we want or expect them to be. And I think it’s somewhat connected to ego, but now we’re getting into some pretty deep territory. But…I like it! I think so, yes, I used to be like that. I used to be. I’m less like that now, and I appreciate difficult moments more because there’s also a lot of good to be found in those moments.

“I mean, we can’t control everything, we can’t expect everything to be perfect because perfection doesn’t teach you anything. I don’t think there’s anything particularly positive about it.

“In the end, we grow a lot through… or we become stronger during difficult times than during good ones. So I’ve largely let go of that kind of perfectionism. And those incredibly high expectations, I don’t like them anymore.”

But is there a positive side to perfectionism for you? Do you think you became the player you are thanks to your perfectionism?

“Yes. This is a struggle I have with myself, for example. In this profession, I believe that perfectionism and ego are two things that drive us to succeed at work, in our professional lives. Ego drives you to be better than, say, the opponent you’re playing against.

“Perfectionism makes you work harder, train better, take better care of yourself and I think that helps you develop a lot professionally. But there has to be a balance. It can’t all be about perfectionism because it makes you incredibly demanding of yourself and when you go through difficult times, you won’t know how to deal with them.

When you make a mistake, are you very demanding and hard on yourself? I mean, how do you treat yourself when something doesn’t go the way you wanted?

“In the past, for example… I’ve changed a great deal. I went through a really difficult time early in my career here in Italy and hit rock bottom, but with outside help, psychological support, I got through it.

“That’s why I keep saying ‘before’. Back then, I was very hard on myself. I didn’t allow myself to fail. If I did, I was extremely negative towards myself, I couldn’t accept that I might fail or make mistakes.

“Now I handle it much better. Now I feel that making mistakes is part of the job, it’s something that helps you improve, something that helps you grow. So I deal with it much more calmly, I process it much better internally.

“I think you still need to hold yourself to high standards and you also need to know how to find a solution to that mistake, whether in your career or in your personal life, but with much more calm and more kindness towards myself.”

This interview is also meant to share some values with others, right? In those moments, what exactly do you tell yourself to be kinder to yourself?

“Well… What a good question! In moments when I’ve gone through difficult situations, perhaps, after that period I was telling you about, I’m aware that everyone can make mistakes. I know that making mistakes is part of the job and it’s what helps me grow.

“So I changed my perspective. I used to see it very negatively, now I find the positive in the negative. So I understand that if I focus on something positive or look at it from a positive perspective, everything surrounding the mistake changes.

“All that noise stops being noise and turns into a sense of calm. It’s normal to make a mistake and be demanding of yourself, to want to avoid making that mistake again, but it might still happen.

“So at that moment, I believe that being kind to yourself and recognising that it’s something that can happen and that you can use it to improve, is, I think, the way forward to avoid falling into negativity. But instead maintain that positivity and balance that can help you feel at peace, as I was saying in there, like the experience I had in there earlier.”

Regarding that difficult period you went through, which helped you grow and taught you so many things, you mentioned therapy. Could you tell me, not so much what happened, but what your experience with therapy was like? I mean, what did it give you at first?

“I sought help from a psychologist because I was going through a very difficult time and couldn’t find a way to move forward. We’re expected to deal with situations… that I find mentally overwhelming, at just 21 years old, when you have no professional experience, because in the end, everything comes at you so fast.

“So I went to a psychologist, and completely changed my perspective. I mean, I started seeing everything negative that happened to me as a step forward, thinking: this is something that will help you improve, something you needed to go through.

“Everything changed when I changed my perspective. I used to be very hard on myself, very hard, I demanded so much of myself. Now I’m someone who feels much more at ease.

“We can all fail, make mistakes, go through difficult situations, So the way I treat myself, the way I respond to myself, the way I talk to myself, I think it plays a crucial role in maintaining a consistently positive mindset.”

Today, with the maturity and mindset you’ve developed, how do you handle pressure? Those moments when expectations are high, when your heart starts beating faster, how do you deal with those moments?

“It depends. Because speaking for myself, I see pressure as something that helps give me that extra push to… I mean, I’m someone who believes that footballers naturally feel pressure or feel a little nervous before a match, even the day before, depending on the match, some matches are more important than others, but you still feel that pressure.

“I think accepting that pressure is positive because it helps prepare you, but I haven’t had situations where pressure has paralysed me, because I experienced that in the past.

“In the past, I’ve felt that kind of pressure, and pressure that paralyses you is very negative because it’s very different from the pressure you feel when you’re in a good place mentally, which helps you prepare.

“It’s a kind of pressure, the pressure I used to feel, that completely paralyses you, it’s a pressure that makes your heart race, that makes you afraid, so they’re two different kinds of pressure. I’ve experienced both.

“The first is difficult to handle because it’s anxiety, the expectation of performing well, it’s the feeling that so many people are watching you, you have to perform well, you have to play well, and that gets into your head, and I don’t think it’s very positive.

“The other, on the other hand, helps you prepare, you feel a little nervous, you get that slight feeling of getting yourself ready, but if you manage to channel it properly, it becomes something that prepares you, a natural response to having something important to face.”

Listening to you speak and watching you play, I see someone who’s very composed. That confidence you have in yourself, have you always had it? Where does it come from?

“I’m someone who has always given the impression of being very confident. I mean, I’ve always believed I had a lot of confidence in myself, but actually, when things got tough, I didn’t have it because whenever I went through a difficult time, I doubted myself a lot.

“I think you develop that through psychological work, but also by feeling confident in your work. Those things go hand in hand. I mean, it’s not all down to the psychologist and nothing to do with my career.

“No. I mean, everything has gone hand in hand. When I started going through this process, things also started going really well for me in football, which helped along the way. So I’ve managed to develop confidence in both areas, which has made me the person I am today, someone who I believe really does have a lot of confidence in himself, because I genuinely feel it.

“It’s something I’ve worked on a lot, learning to believe in yourself, not because of what other people say or the value others place on you, but because of the value you give yourself. And that’s where I’ve found my stability, my peace and my confidence in that environment.

You’ve played alongside some incredible players. How did you manage… I mean, did you use the comparison with their talent as a way to grow rather than feeling envious, as something positive to help you improve?

“Yes. The thing is, this is very closely connected to confidence. You know? When you believe in yourself and have that confidence, you learn to appreciate what you can learn from others. If you’re perhaps someone who doesn’t have much confidence in yourself, you might feel envious of others.

“And then you fail to recognise the lesson that the other person is teaching you, even when you can learn just by watching them. So I began to understand that when I started reaching a place of emotional wellbeing, where I was more focused on the present.

“Before, because I had less confidence in myself, I compared myself to others more. Maybe I didn’t appreciate what someone else was doing or perhaps I couldn’t fully appreciate what they were trying to teach me.

“Once you manage to build a solid sense of confidence and truly believe in yourself, you see what others can teach you in a positive light. And you see it as an opportunity to grow, you look at it from a different perspective.

“So it’s not just about what people might be teaching you directly. I’ve learned from many players just by watching, just by paying attention. But sometimes I’ve learned from negative things too. I mean, not just from positive things. I understand that learning isn’t just about someone saying: ‘Listen, you need to do this, and I think you should do it this way’.

“No, it’s also about how they behave. For example, right now we have Luka Modric in the team. And I pay a lot of attention to him, to how he behaves, to the humility he shows, to how he handles different situations.

“And that’s something you understand when you’re comfortable with yourself. If you’re not comfortable with yourself, I don’t think you’ll be able to understand that. I mean, you won’t see the other person as a positive example. You’ll see them in a negative light.

And when you’re experiencing a great moment, are you able to recognise it? To feel proud of yourself? To enjoy that moment of happiness? To stop and appreciate it?

“That’s something I struggle with, for example. It’s something I find difficult because I’m aware of it, but I think it’s something that people generally struggle with because we tend to notice the negative things more or give more importance to difficult moments than to the positive ones.

“And I think that’s a mistake everyone makes, I don’t know why. But I’m trying to work on it, I’m aware of it. But I have to tell you that if we were to compare how much I enjoy the good moments with how much I suffer during the bad ones, no.

“I suffer more during the bad moments than I enjoy the good ones. And unfortunately, that’s something I still haven’t learned how to manage or how to truly enjoy those positive moments because we’re also here to enjoy the good moments and to experience them fully. But I find that harder than dealing with a difficult moment.”

I really like how much you’ve grown in terms of maturity, everything you’ve come to understand. So I’d like to ask you one last question to reflect on everything. It’s a simple question: How are you?

Not how you are today, but looking at your life, what kind of chapter are you going through right now? Is Mario happy?

Mario is very happy. I mean, this whole conversation we’ve had has a lot to do with the positive place I’m in right now. If I were going through a difficult time, perhaps there are many things I wouldn’t understand the way I do now.

“But I’m in a really good place right now because I’m exactly where I want to be. I’m somewhere I’m appreciated and loved. I became a father a year ago. I have a wife who loves me very much too.

“It’s as though so many things are coming together, things are going well in my career, things are going well with my family. I have friends who I believe are truly valuable people. I also have a family that means so much to me.

“So it’s like everything is going really well right now. So I feel very balanced, I feel very much at peace. I feel like I’m exactly where I want to be. I’m really appreciated. So right now I’m at a very happy point in my life. Very happy.

“If negative things happen, I have a support system I can rely on. I have that support that helps me feel okay. And I think that’s really important because I believe you’ll always experience difficult moments in life. So there’s no way to completely avoid those difficult moments, you can’t, it’s just not possible.

“And life would lose its meaning. But having that safety net and that support system, I think it also allows you to thrive in every other area of your life. So I’m very happy. Right now I feel incredibly happy, very peaceful, very balanced, very happy with myself too, and I’m genuinely very happy we had this conversation because I’m really interested in all these psychological aspects,” he concluded.

#1952. SFA must row back on all-in Sebastien Pocognoli gamble as Scotland fear ultimate custard pie

Taxi for Sebastien Pocognoli? Or should that be cable car? Scotland suffered in Switzerland on Monday and appear to be on a very slippery slope.

Steve Clarke endured two 4-0 defeats in his first five matches in charge so let no one argue that heavy beatings alone are sackable offences. But Pocognoli is sorely aware that he is treading on thin ice in the court of public opinion following a 4-0 drubbing against Switzerland in St Gallen, a gateway to the Alps.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

He won’t need to look at the main Tartan Army fans’ forum, where the most visited thread is titled simply: sack him.

The numbers commenting suggests a healthy debate is occurring. Although a few are backing him, or at least who are pointing out that six games is not long enough to judge anyone, they are in the minority.

Of course, a lot of this is the usual ‘look at me and my extreme opinion’ showboating. Heaven knows, there was enough of that on X in the aftermath of Scotland’s latest reversal. Everyone’s an expert. Everyone knew better although, in the case of Pocognoli, maybe they did.

He was told Ben Gannon-Doak isn’t a wing-back and he was told that what is good for a game against North Macedonia might not necessarily be what is required against a team like Switzerland. The double midfield pivot of Lewis Ferguson and Billy Gilmour? Isn’t working. Again, a conclusion many reached at the end of the last window, long before the wretched night in a charming Swiss hamlet. Once known as the capital of embroidery, St Gallen is where things began unstitching very badly indeed for Scotland’s new manager after a heavy and cheerless defeat.

It was as concerning as it was sore. After all, Switzerland played what their fans explained was a B team and yet still had the game won inside 51 minutes. The "oles" had started. If the Swiss weren’t such a polite lot, we might have been treated to a rendition of: "Are you Liechtenstein in disguise?"

It’s just as well the Nations League format has changed otherwise Scotland could be looking at a relegation play-off against the Faroe Islands – unbeaten in six Nations League games – to avoid demotion to League C.

Scotland are not world beaters but they are better than this. They are better than finishing a distant third in a group where they are ranked seven places higher than the team that did in fact finish in second place: Slovenia. That’s underachievement writ large, whether someone is finding his feet or not. There’s giving a manager time and then there’s expecting the bare minimum.

No wonder there’s anger. No wonder there’s bemusement at the SFA appearing so beholden to the gospel according to Pocognoli that they have permitted his ideas about tactics to cascade throughout the entire set-up. As Under-21 coach Tony Docherty stated a few weeks ago, his side will be a “mirror image” of the A side. Gadzooks. And further down the chain, including the likes of the Under-15s and Under-16s? All working in the same, uniform way, Docherty confirmed.

Memo to the SFA: stop wasting time arranging friendlies in Boston and start rowing back on this one-size-fits-all formula. It could negatively impact Scottish football for generations. In many people's eyes, Pocognoli is already done after a reign lasting barely 90 days.

Getting him out means forking out the compensation fee but it also means telling the phalanx of new coaches – as many as ten have been appointed at various age levels – to ditch the high line, the three defenders and ‘box’ midfield. It means turning Hampden upside down.

It is, nevertheless, a good time to sack someone. If the international window is prime time for clubs to ditch unwanted managers then surely it’s optimal for an international team to do so now: in this long gap between international matches.

Scotland’s next competitive international could be as long away as next September if they are drawn in a four-team group for the Euros. Pocognoli, who turned 39 just before he took the job, could be in his 40s before Scotland next play a match of consequence.

Of course, there is one very important looming date: Sunday 6 December. Pocognoli – or at least we must assume at the time of writing that it will be Pocognoli – will be present and correct in the International Convention Centre in Belfast for the draw for Euro 2028 qualifying.

Ian Maxwell, the SFA chief executive, will be beside him to face some no doubt awkward questions. One of them will be, where are Scotland going? Because from this angle, it looks like backwards. They are at risk of being splatted with international football’s biggest custard pie: failing to qualify for a tournament they are co-hosting. Now assured pot three in the draw, it’s possible they miss out.

The post-World Cup malaise might well have been unavoidable. Even with Clarke in charge there would have been a likely drop-off. The natives were already restless. Away from the traffic cone malarkey, away from the baseball and boozing, it’s been a dreadful year for the national team.

Six defeats out of 13 matches and just five wins, the only one of any real worth being the 1-0 victory over Haiti and even that drew criticism for not being comprehensive enough. Three defeats in six Nations League games, two of which came at Hampden, suggests it’s going from bad to worse under Pocognoli.

The SFA have been criticised for milking the summer trip to Massachusetts to the max, with reports of a biennial friendly match being arranged at Fenway Park or elsewhere. A hat tip to Boston’s boys of summer might be acceptable if Maxwell and co invoke the fundamental rule of baseball in relation to Pocognoli: Three strikes and you’re out. They won’t and neither should they.

Three defeats in six matches is not a sacking offence. But an appointment the SFA seemed very pleased with themselves to acknowledge was data-led now looks increasingly at risk of an outage.

#1950. England versus Spain becoming a new 'clásico' as Leeds United keeper James Trafford announces himself on world stage

That's how widely-respected Spanish sports newspaper Marca described La Roja's rivalry with England following the Three Lions' stunning Sunday-best victory at the Metropolitano. High praise indeed.

That it is becoming one of the most absorbing and significant in world football is surely beyond doubt now.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

In terms of beating the world champions, England have been here before. Back in November 2011, a screamer from Frank Lampard secured a Wembley victory against the feted Spanish, who were also European Championship holders at the same time.

This felt different. On that aforesaid occasion, England prevailed following a backs-to-the-wall performance which saw them pinned back in their own half for long spells against dominant opponents. They converted one of just two chances that came their way.

By contrast, Sunday saw those in white subjugate Spain with an elite showing.

Certainly for 65 to 70 minutes, the hosts' much-vaunted midfield—Arsenal duo Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino, alongside Fabián Ruiz and Alex Baena—were suffocated by England's high press.

It was an intense game plan executed 'with the precision of a master tailor' in the words of Marca. Ruiz and Merino both got the hook at half-time.

The narrative only changed when Elliot Anderson received his marching orders.

The hosts roared back and things became undeniably hairy in the final quarter. But unlike against Argentina in Atlanta in July, Thomas Tuchel's substitutions did not see England adopt a defensive straitjacket.

Leeds United's Dominic Calvert-Lewin came on as the visitors focused on staying higher up the pitch, if at all possible, amid serious late pressure from Spain.

It ended in a merited 3-2 win for the English. In three of the last four meetings between these two, a team has triumphed by the odd goal in five.

England triumphed by the same scoreline and in similar fashion to their previous visit to Spain back in October 2018 - in another Nations League encounter played out in Seville, this time. Again, they achieved success by being proactive as opposed to parking the bus.

Fabulous counter-attacking strikes from Raheem Sterling (2) and Marcus Rashford put the visitors 3-0 up to silence the Spanish hordes. It was the prelude to a strong home fightback in the second half, but no victory.

On this occasion, England's physical and tactical dominance was even more sustained and their third goal, scored by Ben White on 57 minutes, finished off a move of the highest order.

For too long in the past, certainly before that 2018 occasion in Seville, England had been cowed on their visits to Spain. In their previous four matches, all defeats, they failed to score. Ever since Gary Lineker, then at Barcelona, struck all four goals in a stunner at Madrid's Bernebeu Stadium in February 1987.

England have now regained the full respect of international football's undoubted success story of the current century. The team who, alongside France, are the current benchmark for all other nations.

Sunday night was undeniably sweetened by the fact that Spain relinquished their magnificent 44-game unbeaten sequence in the process.

That run included a 2-1 win over England in the Euro 2024 final in Berlin and this summer’s World Cup.

Spain's previous defeat was back in March 2023 against Scotland in Glasgow.

On an evening when the usual suspects came to the party in the shape of Jude Bellingham, whose pass for White's goal was delectable and Harry Kane, others also accepted their invites.

What a night for Leeds's James Trafford for instance. His fantastic double save late on to deny Fer Lopez and Aymeric Laporte announced his arrival on the world stage.

It presents Tuchel with a genuine headache - a welcome one, that said - regarding who will be his bonafide No 1 in 2027.

The battle between Trafford and Jordan Pickford is now a proper fight. It's not quite Peter Shilton versus Ray Clemence levels in the 1970s and early 80s just yet, but it might be heading in that direction. Tellingly, Trafford started both Nations League games against Spain, as opposed to his Everton rival.

Remember, remember the month of November? England will.

Sunday's success was a statement win of the ilk of 2015 when they beat the French 2-0 at Wembley and a decade earlier, in the same month, when a late brace from Michael Owen saw them triumph 3-2 against bitter foes Argentina, in Geneva of all places. Let's hope on this occasion, they build on it.

#1949. Scotland duo set to lose highly rated boss just months after record breaking Scottish Premiership move

A trio of former Scottish Premiership stars are set to lose the manager who took them to the EFL Championship as part of the club’s big summer revamp.

Scotland internationals Stephen Welsh and Ross Stewart both made Bosman free transfer moves to Swansea City in the summer from Celtic and Southampton respectively, while New Zealand forward Elijah Just joined them for a club-record fee of £6million from Motherwell following a stunning debut campaign at Fir Park.

However, the trio are set to see highly rated head coach Vitor Matos complete a shock exit from the club just three months after they arrived in South Wales, with the Portuguese boss said to be edging closer to a move that would see him appointed by Ligue 1 outfit Strasbourg, who are expected to sack current manager Hugo Oliveira, after a run of five defeats in six matches.

Transformed under Matos since his arrival last November, the 38-year-old has enjoyed a strong start to the new campaign and has the second-tier side just three points from the automatic promotion spots in the English second tier, with eight wins in the opening 15 league matches.

The move will come as a major blow for former Celtic and Motherwell centre-back Welsh. A regular starter under Matos since his summer arrival, he credited the former Marítimo boss as a key reason behind his maiden call-up to the Scotland senior squad in September.

A revelation on loan to Motherwell last season under Jens Berthel Askou, the 26-year-old was prized away by Swansea in the summer when his contract at Celtic expired in June. Detailing the reasons for moving across the border, Welsh specifically credited the impact of Matos on his decision.

“They made it clear that they really wanted me,” said Welsh upon his arrival. “With the way the head coach spoke about the club, the environment he wants to create and the way he wants to play; it was a no-brainer. The Championship is a brilliant division, and one I am excited to be playing my football in and challenging myself in. I have experience but I am also young enough to be ready for a new opportunity and a new chapter in my career.”

Meanwhile, former Ross County forward Stewart has found the net once in five games for Swansea, while Welsh’s former Motherwell teammate Just has started eight league games for his new side, assisting one in the 3-1 win over Burnley in September.

Despite his side’s strong start to the EFL Championship campaign, though, Matos looks destined to leave for France, with a switch to the western bank of the Rhine River, with several reports claiming a deal has been agreed for him to become the new Strasbourg head coach. He is expected to sign a deal until the summer of 2028, with a club option for an additional year through 2029.

The expected appointment will see him become Les Bleus' third manager in under a year after Gary O’Neil left to join Ipswich Town just four months after his appointment at Stade de la Meinau. His replacement, the aforementioned Oliveira, has been in charge for just 10 games.

#1948. Erling Haaland speaks out on Manchester City future as financial scandal rumbles on

Erling Haaland says he knows little or nothing about the financial scandal Manchester City are involved and is happy at the club, having signed a contract running until 2034.

In September Manchester City were found guilty of over 100 charges relating to breaches of Premier League financial rules.

City were found to have artificially inflated their financial position by over £900 million from 2009-18.

The club is now appealing those guilty verdict, with a hearing taking place in December and a decision on the appeal expected in early 2027.

If the appeal is unsuccessful than punishment is likely to be severe, with points deductions and fines likely and even expulsion from the Premier League a possibility.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

Manchester City’s players have not said much about the situation and continue to compete, although three league defeats on the spin to Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest may suggest the situation is taking its toll.

Haaland, though, says he has not even looked into the scandal much, pointing out that he was not at the club during the period of time that has been under investigation.

The 26-year-old scored in Norway’s 3-1 win over Wales on Saturday in Oslo and after successfully converting from the penalty spot, he successfully dodged the issue while speaking to TV2.

‘The investigation covered 2009 to 2018,’ he said. ‘In 2009, I played for Bryne U9s. In 2010, the U10s. In 2011, the U11s. 2012, the U12s, 2012, the U13s. Shall we continue? We don’t need the whole list…2014, the U14s. 2015, the U15s and the national team.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

‘Then the U16s, I think. In 2016, I moved up to Bryne’s first team, second team and youth team. In 2017, I went to Molde. In 2018, I was with Molde. The first team, Molde 2 and a bit with the youth team.

‘So this is a question I struggle to answer because it’s a legal battle…It’s a case between the Premier League and Manchester City that a panel will deal with.

‘Am I supposed to answer that? I’m not really sure.’

The iconic striker then joked that these questions should be put to his compatriots that were at Manchester City during the time period in question.

Haaland dug out some names that only die hard Manchester City fans wil remember, saying: ‘There were quite a few Norwegians at the club during that period, I think.

‘Abdisalam Ibrahim, Martin Samuelsen and Omar Elabdellaoui were there. Kjetil Haug was there too. I think there were a couple more but I can’t remember.

‘But it’s a difficult question to answer when I don’t really know that much about it. I assume the answers will come… I don’t know when. I haven’t read much about it.

‘To be completely honest, I’m focused on trying to perform for Manchester City. A club I signed a five-year deal with in 2022 and a new nine-and-a-half-year deal in late 2024. I think that says everything.’

Haaland stuck to his guns when asked about his thoughts on his future amid the ongoing appeal process.

‘I understand that you want a little headline here, but as I said, I signed a long-term contract in 2024,’ he said. ‘I’d say I made a pretty good choice by joining City in 2022. We can all agree on that.

‘I won’t say it myself, but look at the trophies I’ve won and how I’ve developed on and off the pitch. I’m standing here after winning an international 3-1 and we’re top of our group in Europe.

‘Things aren’t going so well for City in the league, but we’ll try to turn that around against Fulham. But we can’t focus on that now. Now we have to focus on Denmark.’

#1945. Declan Rice fires back at Graeme Souness after criticism from Liverpool legend

Declan Rice has fired back at Graeme Souness after stinging criticism, suggesting the Liverpool legend doesn’t understand how football has changed.

Rice is an integral player for England and Premier League champions Arsenal, widely recognised as one of the best midfielders in the world.

However, Souness has his own view and is not entirely sold on the talents of the 27-year-old, who he believes plays too deep to be considered a complete midfielder.

‘How many times do you see him as the last man with the ball? In the build-up, he’s last man,’ Souness said on Piers Morgan’s Football Uncensored. ‘He’s sitting between two centre-halves or between the centre-half and the full-back. He’s last man. A lot of the time, he doesn’t play in midfield.

‘It’s old man’s football. It’s cheating. An old man’s way of playing midfield. You get the ball under no pressure and you play it out to the full-back.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

He plays too deep to affect the game. I don’t think he’s got enough football. Let me tell you what he can do. He’s the best defensive midfielder in the country right now, he smells danger. But then again, he’s back there all the time.

In 323 Premier League outings for West Ham and Arsenal, Rice has scored 25 goals and provided 35 assists.

He is yet to scored in the top flight during the current campaign, but his five assists are more than any other player in the division.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

Responding to the criticism from Souness, Rice said: ‘My numbers since I joined Arsenal speak for themselves. For a “centre back”, I think that’s not bad numbers. I’ve had a lot of assists, a lot of goals. To be a top-class centre back getting those numbers, I’m delighted with that!’

‘Look, Graeme’s got his opinion. I think he’s had his opinion since my West Ham days. I’ve seen his views. I can’t change his opinion. I can only do what I do, which is go on the pitch, perform, play well and block out the noise.’

Rice pointed out that there are different requirements placed in players in the modern game, using Harry Kane’s pitch-trotting exploits as an example.

‘If you speak about the positioning, the “old man’s football”, look at Harry Kane, for instance,’ he said. ‘We played him the other week [Bayern Munich 2-2 Arsenal] and he dropped next to the centre backs 20-30 times to pick up the ball.

‘The game is different now. It’s what the game demands, to get away from your man, to go into different areas to create overloads, to create two v ones, to progress the ball up the pitch. Football is way different. It’s changed a lot, and you’re always trying to look for tactical advantages.

Declan Rice hit TWO worldie free-kicks vs Real Madrid 🤯So nice he did it twice ✌️ pic.twitter.com/zg5CzlQQNh

‘In terms of me as a midfielder, I’m constantly watching clips with Mikel (Arteta). He’s constantly coaching me on the pitch. How I can progress the ball from deep, drop next to the goalkeeper, go to full back to get on the ball, to take the ball up the pitch.

‘So, I feel like we’re now seeing something totally different to what he would see, but in his time football was different. He was a top-class midfielder who won lots of stuff. There’s no argument against him. As a pundit, as a person, his career, you have to respect what he’s done.

‘I didn’t get to see him play, but obviously his accolades were top, and I’ve never got to meet him in person. If I did, there would be no disrespect. I’d shake his hand. I’d chat with him. It’s an opinion at the end of the day. It’s football.’

#1943. Mauricio Pochettino sends message to Sir Alex Ferguson ahead of Man Utd mission

Mauricio Pochettino would welcome the chance to speak with Sir Alex Ferguson as he prepares for the task of resurrecting Manchester United.

Michael Carrick’s successor’s penultimate match in charge of United States ended in an emphatic 6-0 thrashing of Haiti as he moved a step closer to beginning his United tenure.

The former Tottenham boss will start life at the Red Devils on Wednesday after two Nations League matches with Haiti, but USA all but assured their place in the semi-finals of the competition with a comprehensive first-leg showing.

Austin Trusty’s smart finish from a 10th-minute set-piece ensured Pochettino’s team were ahead at half-time before they ran riot after the break with Christian Pulisic able to net a brace either side of goals from Julian Hall, Weston McKennie and Folarin Balogun ahead of Tuesday’s second leg.

Pochettino paid tribute to his staff and players in an emotional press conference on Friday and duly watched USA romp to a 6-0 victory.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

‘We played for him,’ Trusty said in a post-match interview with TNT Sports after opening the scoring in the 10th minute.

‘Obviously, he’s our gaffer. Obviously it’s sad that he’s moving on. It’s a great opportunity that he’s moving on to. But we played for him. It’s his team. It’s his identity, and the mindset is to win every single game, every single match.’

The second leg of the Nations League quarterfinals will take place Tuesday in Cincinnati.

‘Pochettino is an amazing manager and he added a lot to us with the national team,’ Folarin Balogun told TNT Sports. ‘It’s always sad to see a top coach leave but it’s a part of the sport.’

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

The 54-year-old will have little time to reflect on his accomplishments in his soon-to-be former role as he will immediately begin plotting for his first game in charge of United at Anfield next Sunday.

Pochettino inherits a side that is currently in the bottom three in the Premier League table, short on confidence and a dressing room split following the recent actions of senior players, including the likes of Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez.

Given the current state of play and his pre-existing relationship with Ferguson, it is perhaps no surprise that Pochettino is seeking the advice of the club’s greatest ever manager as he prepares to embark on arguably the toughest assignment of his managerial career to date.

‘Not yet, but for sure I will have the opportunity after Tuesday,’ Pochettino told Telegraph Sport when asked if he had been in contact with Ferguson.

‘I said many years ago and always I say the same – for me, Sir Alex Ferguson represents everything that I admire from a coach, a head coach, a man, a manager and I think he represents my values. I really admire him.

‘For sure, from Tuesday, we will have the possibility to talk – if I will have time because it’s going to be very intense.

‘But if there’s the possibility to talk, then of course I will do that.’

#1942. ‘Build slowly’ - Leeds United told what would constitute success this season by ex-Whites defender Danny Mills

Consolidation in the Premier League would constitute a successful season for Leeds United, according to former Whites defender Danny Mills.

Leeds sit ninth in the table after 10 games and have taken already taken points off the likes of Manchester United, Tottenham Hotspur and Brighton & Hove Albion.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Some pundits have suggested the Whites could push for European football, but Mills believes the securing of safety at the earliest point possible takes precedence.

The 49-year-old, who represented Leeds between 1994 and 2004, told BOYLE Sports, who offer the latest football odds: “I think what Leeds did last season was to fall into a formation that worked for them.

“They're high energy, they're aggressive, they're physical, and they've caused teams a lot of problems.

“What would be success for Leeds this season? Safe by March, I would say. The second season in the Premier League, if you can consolidate again, then you start to go, right, okay, now we're here and hopefully here for a while and you build slowly.

“They did fantastically well last season to stay up. Now you're looking at them going, okay, they're solid. They don't get beat easily. It's a fantastic basis to work from.”

Leeds have enjoyed success with the use of a flexible 3-4-2-1 formation, with the system spearheaded by talismanic frontman Dominic Calvert-Lewin.

Mills said: “They've got a formation that's worked, they've recruited for that formation. They will be difficult to beat, and they will cause teams problems with their athleticism in the wide areas. Dominic Calvert-Lewin up front as well.

“They do have replacements and they might even look in January thinking, ‘okay, it looks like we're gonna be safe’. They might even recruit, you know, whether it be a back-up or someone to assist Dominic Calvert-Lewin in that area. I think they're in a strong position at the moment.”

#1939. Bruno Fernandes gives Man Utd Mauricio Pochettino ultimatum over new contract

Bruno Fernandes will delay any decision on a new Manchester United contract until he has made up his mind on new manager Mauricio Pochettino.

The 32-year-old’s current deal expires at the end of the season, although the club has an option to extend his contract by another year.

With Fernandes already rejecting two offers of a new deal, the Red Devils are expected to trigger the 12-month extension to avoid him agreeing a move abroad on a free transfer, which he would be able to do in the last six months of his contract.

The Sun report that Manchester United remain confident Fernandes will sign a new contract, but that his decision is based on how things play out under new boss Pochettino.

The Portuguese star has cut a frustrated figure so far this season under Michael Carrick, playing well below his capabilities as the whole team has struggled.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

Carrick has been axed and Pochettino returns to the Premier League for a fourth job, having managed Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea.

Not only is Fernandes waiting to see what working under the Argentine is like, but also whether the hierarchy will back the new boss in the transfer market.

The Red Devils signed Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos over the summer, but failed to strengthen at the back or up front.

The midfield has been revamped, but United look very short at full-back and centre-forward, while they are well stocked at centre-back, but their options continue to perform poorly.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

If Fernandes is to remain at Old Trafford beyond this season, he will have to see some intent in the transfer market from the decision-makers at the club.

Pochettino is expected to want to make significant changes to the playing squad at Old Trafford, both in terms of outgoings and incomings.

Like Fernandes, Lisandro Martinez and Harry Maguire see their current deals expire in the summer of 2027 but the club can extend them by another year. Big decisions are to be made on both.

Luke Shaw is also into the final few months of his current contract, with the experienced left-back currently sidelined with injury.

Work on the squad will begin in the winter transfer window, with Pochettino arriving to take charge next week after finishing his time in charge of USA.

Speaking of his choice to leave America for Manchester, he said: ‘It’s difficult to talk now. I’m a very emotional guy. It’s a very sad decision.

‘But we are professionals and we are trying to make our dreams come true.

‘They [US Soccer Federation] know that not many opportunities can happen in your career like a side the size of Manchester United. When that arrives, it’s difficult to turn down.’
